course_goals.text: Master the foundational principles and mechanics of deep learning, including core architectures, training dynamics, and optimization theory.
Analyze and apply advanced techniques for representation learning, data generation, and model adaptation across various domains.
Evaluate the theoretical limits and practical robustness of deep learning models, focusing on generalization, scaling, and inference.

concepts.name: Differential programming
concepts.definition: Differential programming is a programming paradigm where parts of the program are parameterized. This allows gradient-based optimization to tune those parameters to optimize the program or find a local optimum.

concepts.name: Pointwise non-linearity
concepts.definition: Pointwise non-linearity is a type of nonlinear function used in neural networks to map outputs. These non-linearities are typically applied to each component of the output vector individually.

concepts.name: Generative model
concepts.definition: Generative models are systems designed to handle uncertainty in the output space, moving beyond the single point predictions made by standard neural nets. Modern approaches often achieve this by modeling simple distributions, such as Gaussian distributions, conditioned on a large amount of input information.

concepts.name: Transfer learning
concepts.definition: Transfer learning is the technique of reusing components from a previously trained model. This allows knowledge learned for one task, such as categorizing animals, to be applied to a different task, like satellite imagery.

concepts.name: Deep learning
concepts.definition: Deep learning is a field of study interested in modeling complex phenomena in the real world. It is presented as a possible solution for tackling the difficulty of modeling these complex systems.

concepts.name: Complex phenomena
concepts.definition: Complex phenomena are real-world subjects, such as natural language, images, DNA, and climate change, that are characterized by their inherent complexity. These phenomena are the types of systems we seek to model using deep learning.

concepts.name: Artificial Intelligence
concepts.definition: Amortized inference is a method of solving a problem where training learns a set of weights that directly solves the problem without needing to go through a step-by-step reasoning process.

concepts.name: Perceptron
concepts.definition: Perceptron is the first neural network, which was designed to recognize or categorize images. This basic unit forms the building block for most of the deep learning used today.

concepts.name: Backpropagation
concepts.definition: Backpropagation is a fundamental concept that enables multilayer perceptrons to be reasonably trained. This concept allows a gradient to be propagated through multiple layers of perceptrons.

concepts.name: Multilayer perceptron
concepts.definition: Multilayer perceptron is a structure consisting of multiple perceptrons stacked on top of each other. This structure allows the network to solve categorization problems that are not separable from a linear classifier.

concepts.name: Convolutional neural network
concepts.definition: A convolutional network is essentially a locally connected network where the same weights are used regardless of where the initial input values are coming from. This structure allows the model to process local functions of the input.

concepts.name: ImageNet
concepts.definition: ImageNet was the first very large-scale data set of its kind, serving as a vital component that allowed machine learning to achieve significant breakthroughs.

concepts.name: Non-linearity
concepts.definition: Non-linearity is the function applied between layers that allows a network to model complex, non-straight relationships. Without this non-linearity, stacking multiple linear layers simply results in a single linear combination.

concepts.name: Modular reuse
concepts.definition: Modular reuse is the concept within an open source community where trained weights from one architecture can be taken and used as a module within a larger system. This larger system may incorporate many different components pulled from various sources.

concepts.name: Gradient descent
concepts.definition: Gradient descent is an optimization technique used to minimize a cost function by finding the optimal set of model parameters. This process involves calculating the gradient and then updating the model weights in the direction of that gradient.

concepts.name: Parameter
concepts.definition: Parameter: Parameters of a model are defined as all the different layers of weights and all the different layers of biases within the model structure.

concepts.name: Linear layer
concepts.definition: Linear layer is a building block in neural networks where a component of the output representation is calculated as a sum over inputs multiplied by corresponding weights. This calculation can also incorporate a bias term.

concepts.name: Bias term
concepts.definition: Bias term is a component added to the calculation that does not take in any of the input components. It serves as a constant offset in the linear combination.

concepts.name: Rectified linear unit
concepts.definition: Rectified linear unit (ReLU) is a pointwise non-linearity defined as the maximum of zero and the input value $z$. This function is super efficient to implement and is widely used in current models.

concepts.name: Representational power
concepts.definition: Representational power is the theoretical ability of a model to map and represent complex functions. With two or more layers and non-linearity, a deep network can theoretically represent any function.

concepts.name: Capacity
concepts.definition: Capacity refers to the amount of complexity or number of dimensions a model can handle. Given sufficient capacity, a model can theoretically approximate any function.

concepts.name: Deep network
concepts.definition: Deep network is a type of neural network that represents data in a more compact way, allowing it to encode knowledge efficiently. This representation is considered an improvement over previous methods like lookup tables.

concepts.name: Shallow network
concepts.definition: Shallow network is a network structure that, if not sufficiently wide, may only be able to efficiently compute simple tasks, such as finding edges. In contrast, a deep network can efficiently compute much harder tasks.

concepts.name: Overparameterized
concepts.definition: Overparameterized describes a new paradigm in deep learning, replacing the classical concepts of underfitting and overfitting. This term refers to models that possess a very large number of parameters.

concepts.name: Generalize
concepts.definition: Generalize is the ability of a model to learn rules that apply broadly, rather than merely memorizing the training data. This allows the model to perform well on data that it has not seen before.

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.definition: Overfitting is the phenomenon where a model learns patterns from the training data so perfectly that it generalizes poorly to new, unseen data. This occurs when the model is too complex, resulting in a 'spiky' or 'peaky' function that fits the training points exactly.

concepts.name: Cross-entropy loss
concepts.definition: Cross-entropy loss indicates the distance between the distribution the model predicts and the actual input distribution, which is typically a one-hot encoding. Cross-entropy loss tells the network to maximize the probability of the training data, which forces the output to be a reasonably good probability model of the object class, assuming sufficient training data.

concepts.name: One hot encoding
concepts.definition: One hot encoding is a vector representation used for the ground truth label, where every element is zero except for the correct class, which is marked with a one.

concepts.name: Tensor
concepts.definition: A tensor is a multi-dimensional matrix that serves as the mathematical representation of the input data and the layers within the model. Essentially, everything in the deep learning model is represented as a tensor.

concepts.name: Representation learning
concepts.definition: Representation learning is the process that operates in the encoding direction of a neural network. It aims to find an effective mapping from raw data to useful embeddings.

concepts.name: Neural network
concepts.definition: Neural network is a structure consisting of a chain of different blocks or layers. Each of these layers has associated parameters that are used during the training process.

concepts.name: Loss
concepts.definition: Loss is a function defined over all of the data points. Loss serves as a mechanism for evaluating the optimality of the model's performance.

concepts.name: Optimal set of theta
concepts.definition: Optimal set of theta is the specific set of parameters that minimizes the loss function. This minimization must occur across all of the available data set.

concepts.name: Cost function
concepts.definition: Cost function is a measure that quantifies the total loss across all data points in the training data set, which gradient descent seeks to minimize.

concepts.name: Gradient
concepts.definition: Gradient is a mathematical measure that indicates the direction of maximal change for a parameter set, which is used in optimization algorithms.

concepts.name: Learning rate (eta)
concepts.definition: Learning rate (eta) is a defined value that determines how far the parameters will step in the direction of the gradient during each iteration.

concepts.name: Loss landscape
concepts.definition: Loss landscape is the surface that represents the cost function, and it is where the optimization process begins and moves to find a minimum.

concepts.name: Stochastic gradient descent
concepts.definition: Stochastic gradient descent is an optimization method that approximates the total gradient by calculating it over a small subset of the data. This approach is used because calculating the gradient over the entire dataset is often computationally intractable.

concepts.name: Batch
concepts.definition: A batch is a subset of the data that is used to compute the gradient at any given point during the training process. The size of the batch determines how many examples are used before the parameters are updated.

concepts.name: Overall loss function
concepts.definition: The overall loss function is the total measure of error that the model attempts to minimize. This function is typically calculated as a sum of the individual losses across every single example in the training data.

concepts.name: Implicit regularizer
concepts.definition: Implicit regularizer is a property of stochastic gradient descent where the inherent noise provides a benefit to the training process. The noise helps the model bounce out of local minima, assisting the search for a global minimum.

concepts.name: Local minima
concepts.definition: Local minima are points in the loss landscape where the optimization process may become trapped, preventing it from reaching the global minimum. Depending on the starting point of the optimization, the process might settle into one of these suboptimal points.

concepts.name: Momentum
concepts.definition: Momentum is a technique in gradient descent that biases gradient steps to continue in the direction of previous updates. This gives the optimization process momentum based on its past direction of movement.

concepts.name: Hyperparameter
concepts.definition: Hyperparameter is a value, such as alpha, that determines the strength of momentum. The strength of that momentum can either help or hurt the optimization process.

concepts.name: Differentiable
concepts.definition: Differentiable describes a property of a function, such as a loss landscape, that possesses a derivative. A function can be differentiable even if it is flat, meaning it still has a defined derivative at that point.

concepts.name: Exploding gradients
concepts.definition: Exploding gradient occurs when the gradient increases toward infinity as the minimizer is approached. This results in highly unstable updates, making it difficult to actually hit the minimum.

concepts.name: Vanishing gradient
concepts.definition: Vanishing gradient is a condition where the gradient becomes extremely small as the minimum is approached, causing the training progress to be very slow. This slow progress can be dominated by noise in the training batches.

concepts.name: Multiple local minima
concepts.definition: Multiple local minima refers to a loss landscape that is not guaranteed to be convex, meaning it may contain several low-loss regions. When this occurs, the initial model parameters greatly influence which minimum the optimization process finds.

concepts.name: Convexity
concepts.definition: Convexity is a property of a function, such as a loss landscape, that allows for the assumption of a single minimum. When a function is convex, all gradients point toward that single minimum.

concepts.name: Evolution strategy
concepts.definition: Evolution strategy is a gradient-like method that finds locally loss-minimizing directions in parameter space. It achieves this by sampling small perturbations around existing parameter values and moving toward perturbations that achieve lower loss.

concepts.name: Gradient clipping
concepts.definition: Gradient clipping is a mechanism used to help manage peakiness or pointiness in a loss function. It works by scaling back the gradient if it exceeds a predefined large value, essentially placing a clipping filter on the gradient.

concepts.name: Gaussian error linear unit
concepts.definition: Gaussian error linear unit (GeLU) is a non-linearity that takes the parameters multiplied by the cumulative distribution function for the Gaussian distribution. This function is everywhere continuous, everywhere differentiable, and everywhere smooth.

concepts.name: Loss function
concepts.definition: Loss function is a cost measure that can sometimes have negative values, depending on how it is set up. When minimizing a cost, the function's landscape is not guaranteed to be convex everywhere, meaning it may have parts that go up and down.

concepts.name: Computation graph
concepts.definition: Computation graph is a graph of different functional transformations where each transformation is represented as a node. Stringing these nodes together allows for the performance of useful computation.

concepts.name: Directed acyclic graph
concepts.definition: Directed acyclic graph is a graph where information flows only in one direction along any given edge, and the graph contains no loops or cycles.

concepts.name: Forward pass
concepts.definition: Forward pass is the process of sending data forward through the network. This involves computing the outputs and calculating the overall loss.

concepts.name: Cost
concepts.definition: Cost is the overall calculation of the loss across all of the data. Cost is also a mechanism used to evaluate the optimality of the model.

concepts.name: Jacobian formulation
concepts.definition: The Jacobian formulation is a method used to calculate the partial derivative when the output is a vector and the input is a vector. This formulation results in a matrix whose size is determined by the size of the output by the size of the input.

concepts.name: Partial derivative
concepts.definition: Partial derivative is the rate of change of an output function with respect to a specific input element, resulting in a vector or matrix whose dimensions are determined by the size of the output and input variables. For instance, if the output is a scalar and the input is a matrix, the resulting partial derivative is a matrix where the rows and columns are transposed relative to the input matrix.

concepts.name: Chain rule
concepts.definition: The chain rule is a method used to find the derivative of a composite function, where one function is nested inside another. It involves multiplying the derivative of the outer function by the derivative of the inner function.

concepts.name: Backwards pass
concepts.definition: Backward pass computes the loss derivatives iteratively from top to bottom. The process involves taking partial derivatives with respect to the output and input to calculate the change in parameters.

concepts.name: Layer output gradient (L)
concepts.definition: Layer output gradient (L) is a matrix that tracks the gradient of the layer outputs with regard to the layer inputs. This matrix indicates which way the parameters need to change to move in the maximal direction of optimization.

concepts.name: Cost gradient (g)
concepts.definition: Cost gradient (g) is a row vector representing the gradient of the cost with respect to the activations. This vector essentially states the partial derivative of the cost with respect to the input of that layer.

concepts.name: Merging
concepts.definition: Merging is an operation that combines functional components to move forward through a directed-acyclic graph. When propagating a gradient back through a merge, one must track the gradient with respect to the correct input variables.

concepts.name: Branching
concepts.definition: Branching is the process of splitting up or duplicating information within a network. When propagating a gradient back through a branch, the gradients from both paths are summed and sent back through the input.

concepts.name: Parameter sharing
concepts.definition: Parameter sharing occurs when the same set of weights is utilized by multiple components within a network, rather than having separate parameters for each component in a chain. This technique allows for the reuse of weights, such as those pre-trained on large datasets, across different parts of the model.

concepts.name: Software 2.0
concepts.definition: Software 2.0 is a concept where the software defines a space of possible systems, and the goal is to optimize within that space to build the specific system needed to solve a problem.

concepts.name: Feature engineering
concepts.definition: Feature engineering is a process where humans build explicit constraints into how the data might be processed before it is fed into a simple neural network.

concepts.name: Optimizing inputs
concepts.definition: Optimizing inputs is the process of adjusting the input data, such as changing input pixels, to achieve a desired outcome while the network's parameters remain fixed. This approach contrasts with the standard method of changing the network's internal parameters.

concepts.name: Embedding
concepts.definition: Embedding is a mapping that transforms a high-dimensional or complex input, such as an image, into a low-dimensional representation. Embedding is essentially the use of a pre-trained neural network to provide a low-rank representation of the input data.

concepts.name: Universal function approximator
concepts.definition: Universal function approximator is the statement that a neural network can approximate any function that we are interested in, which raises questions about how to make decisions regarding the network's architecture.

concepts.name: Approximation
concepts.definition: Approximation is the process of representing a function by summing up a collection of indicator functions. The height of each rectangle in this sum is determined by a coefficient, $\alpha_i$.

concepts.name: Weierstrass' function
concepts.definition: Weierstrass' function is a classic mathematical function that is everywhere continuous but nowhere differentiable. This characteristic makes it a prime example of a pathological function.

concepts.name: Fractal function
concepts.definition: A fractal function is a function that is defined recursively and is self-similar. This means that if any part of the function is magnified, it resembles the entire function.

concepts.name: Approximation problem
concepts.definition: The approximation problem asks whether a neural network within a specified family can fit a function from a target family of curves to a small error. This formalizes the question of whether a neural network can represent a given set of functions.

concepts.name: L-infinity error
concepts.definition: L-infinity error is a metric used to measure the maximum discrepancy between two functions across all possible inputs. This measure quantifies the largest absolute difference between the two functions anywhere on the input space, unlike measures like the L1 measure which integrate the total difference.

concepts.name: L-Lipschitz function
concepts.definition: L-Lipschitz function is a type of function that has bounded derivatives. This property restricts the rate at which the function can change across its domain.

concepts.name: Norm
concepts.definition: A norm is a mathematical function used to measure the size or length of a vector. It allows us to quantify how large a vector is.

concepts.name: RMS norm
concepts.definition: The RMS norm is a specific type of vector norm defined as the square root of (1/d) times the sum of the coordinates squared. This norm is used to measure the size of a vector.

concepts.name: Euclidean norm
concepts.definition: Euclidean norm is one method used to measure the size of a vector. This norm is characterized as a dimensional object, which distinguishes it from related measures like the RMS norm, which serves as a non-dimensional analog.

concepts.name: Hypercube
concepts.definition: Hypercube is the domain or input space, which is abstractly defined as the set of points in d-dimensional space where all axes are constrained between 0 and 1. It serves as the input space for the functions being approximated.

concepts.name: Three-layer ReLU network
concepts.definition: Three-layer ReLU network is a specific neural network structure defined by having three weight matrices. This architecture includes two intermediate value functions that follow the first and second weight matrices, while the third weight matrix does not utilize a ReLU activation function.

concepts.name: Integral notion of error
concepts.definition: Integral notion of error is a measure of approximation quality that sums up all the absolute differences between the neural network's output and the target function g. This summation is performed across all the little pieces of the domain.

concepts.name: Number of units
concepts.definition: Number of units refers to the total count of neurons within the ReLU Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). This count includes all neurons across the network's layers.

concepts.name: Lipschitz constant
concepts.definition: Lipschitz constant is the measure of the sensitivity between the input and output of a module. When modules are composed in series, these constants multiply, which is an intuitive property of function composition.

concepts.name: Hyperrectangle
concepts.definition: Hyperrectangle is the multidimensional generalization of a rectangle, which is used to partition the input space when dealing with multiple inputs.

concepts.name: Two-layer ReLU network
concepts.definition: A two-layer ReLU network is a type of neural network structure that uses the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation function and involves two layers of computation. This structure is used to approximate complex functions, such as a rectangle.

concepts.name: Indicator
concepts.definition: Indicator is a function that returns 1 if the input value falls within a specific interval, and 0 otherwise. Indicator functions are used as building blocks to construct the function approximation.

concepts.name: Approximation error
concepts.definition: Approximation error is the measure of the difference or 'gap' between the original function and its approximation. This error can be bounded based on the number of strips and the Lipschitz constant.

concepts.name: L1 error
concepts.definition: L1 error of the function approximation is quantified by the total area of the error triangles across all strips. The total error corresponds to summing the maximum possible area of the triangle in each strip.

concepts.name: Error cap
concepts.definition: Error cap represents the height of the region where the hyperrectangle deviates from the surface G. This height generalizes the concept of error from the one-dimensional approximation case.

concepts.name: Surface
concepts.definition: Surface is the visualization of a function $g$ that accepts multiple inputs and yields a single output. This concept generalizes the two-input case into higher dimensions, allowing for the approximation of the function's error integral.

concepts.name: Indicator function
concepts.definition: Indicator function is a function that returns a value of 1 if the input lies within a specific interval or region, and 0 otherwise. This function is used to symbolically represent a geometric shape in a weighted sum.

concepts.name: Stone-Weierstrass theorem
concepts.definition: Stone-Weierstrass theorem is a classic result that demonstrates how polynomials can be used to approximate any continuous function. This theorem is related to the mathematical branch of approximation theory.

concepts.name: Taylor's expansion
concepts.definition: Taylor's expansion is a valid mathematical method for approximating a function by fitting a Taylor series up to a certain degree. This method is similar to the Weierstrass concept of using polynomials to fit a continuous function.

concepts.name: Width
concepts.definition: Width is a key structural parameter of a neural network, referring to the size of its layers. To ensure the network can approximate any function, the width must be at least as large as the dimension of the input space.

concepts.name: Depth
concepts.definition: Depth refers to the number of layers in a neural network. The segment discusses how small depth networks can sometimes be sufficient to fit any function.

concepts.name: Depth separation result
concepts.definition: A depth separation result is a finding that deeper networks can fit certain kinds of functions using significantly fewer neurons. This efficiency is attributed to the compositionality inherent in deeper network architectures.

concepts.name: Piecewise linear function
concepts.definition: A piecewise linear function is a function that, when broken into segments, consists of segments that are linear. These linear segments are then stitched together to form the complete function.

concepts.name: Kink
concepts.definition: Kink is a point in a piecewise linear function where the derivative is discontinuous. These points represent locations where the derivative of the function suddenly changes value.

concepts.name: ReLU network
concepts.definition: ReLU network is a neural network structure whose overall function is piecewise linear because the ReLU function is essentially a linear function with a threshold, and this property is preserved under standard operations like addition and multiplication.

concepts.name: Layer
concepts.definition: A layer is a component within a deep ReLU network that transforms the function from the previous layer. This transformation involves applying the ReLU function to the result of multiplying the previous function by a weight matrix and adding a bias.

concepts.name: Upper bound
concepts.definition: An upper bound is a mathematical limit that describes the maximum possible growth rate of a property, such as the number of kinks. The segment shows that this bound grows polynomially in width but exponentially in depth.

concepts.name: Loss
concepts.definition: Loss is the test loss, which is the metric used to measure how well the model is performing. The loss must eventually go to zero.

concepts.name: Confounding issue
concepts.definition: Confounding issue is some aspect of the training pipeline that we do not fully understand. Such an issue still has a bearing on the results, making it difficult to resolve experimental questions about network scaling or architecture.

concepts.name: Very wide shallow neural net
concepts.definition: Very wide shallow neural net is a three-layer network that, when sufficiently wide, possesses the capacity to approximate any function within a broad class of functions. This contrasts with deeper networks, which can fit certain functions using significantly fewer neurons due to their compositional structure.

concepts.name: Sequential structure
concepts.definition: Sequential structure refers to data where the elements are inherently ordered in a specific sequence, such as a waveform.

concepts.name: Two-dimensional structure
concepts.definition: Two-dimensional structure refers to data that possesses inherent spatial dimensions, such as an image.

concepts.name: Universal approximator
concepts.definition: Universal approximator is a property of a model that allows it to approximate any mathematical function.

concepts.name: Inductive biases
concepts.definition: Inductive biases are the inherent assumptions baked into a model, which dictate what structure or intuition the model assumes about the function it is trying to learn.

concepts.name: Dense layer
concepts.definition: Dense layer, also known as a fully connected layer, is a type of layer where every neuron in the previous layer is connected to every neuron in the current layer. When processing structured data like images, this architecture requires the input to be flattened into a single long vector before computation.

concepts.name: Convolutional layers
concepts.definition: Convolutional layers are a type of layer that processes input data using filters, which allows the same parameters to be used across the entire input data. Convolutional layers are built to be equivariant to translation, meaning the output shifts if the input shifts.

concepts.name: Hypothesis space
concepts.definition: Hypothesis space is a defined subset of all possible models, which adds structure to the model itself. This space shines a spotlight on a specific portion of the overall space of all possible models.

concepts.name: Architectures
concepts.definition: Architectures are structures that enable a model to generalize outside of the training distribution. A good architecture must be able to represent the true function of the data while remaining otherwise minimal.

concepts.name: Sinusoidal activation space
concepts.definition: Sinusoidal activation space is a model type that utilizes sinusoidal activations. This type of activation space is particularly efficient for fitting image data.

concepts.name: Generalization out of distribution
concepts.definition: Generalization out of distribution refers to the model's ability to perform well in regions outside the data distribution, which is distinct from merely fitting the data points where training data exists.

concepts.name: Semantic segmentation
concepts.definition: Semantic segmentation is an application of encoder-decoder architectures where the desired output space must possess spatial extent, distinguishing it from tasks that only produce a single category.

concepts.name: Patch
concepts.definition: Patch is a small piece of the image that is subdivided and used as input for a classifier. Using patches allows the model to classify local regions of the image.

concepts.name: Translation invariant
concepts.definition: Translation invariant describes a property where the classification or category of an object remains the same regardless of its location within the image. This means that an object, such as a bird, should maintain its category even if it is moved from the top corner to the center of the image.

concepts.name: Equivariant mapping
concepts.definition: Equivariant mapping is a type of mapping where applying a translation to the input results in a corresponding translation of the function's output. This property ensures that the model maintains a consistent relationship between input and output under spatial shifts.

concepts.name: Convolution
concepts.definition: Convolution is a linear, shift-invariant transformation applied to grid-structured input data. Essentially, convolution is a method used in signal processing to perform filtering.

concepts.name: Convolutional kernel
concepts.definition: Convolutional kernel is a set of linear weights (W) used to compute a weighted sum of pixels within a patch of data. This kernel functions as a filter, enabling a linear, shift-invariant transformation of grid-structured input data.

concepts.name: Filter
concepts.definition: Filter is the set of weights used to take a linear weighted sum of the input data. This filter is designed to look for specific patterns within the input data.

concepts.name: Toeplitz matrix
concepts.definition: A Toeplitz matrix is a specific form of matrix that arises when the weight matrix is sparse and the values are the same along the entire diagonal. This structure is characteristic of certain convolutional layers.

concepts.name: Equivariant to translation
concepts.definition: Translation equivariance is a property where if the input data is shifted or translated, the resulting output is translated by the same amount. This property is achieved in convolution due to weight sharing.

concepts.name: Receptive field
concepts.definition: Receptive field is the area of the input image that influences a specific output unit. This field increases as more layers are added to the model's depth.

concepts.name: Patch processing
concepts.definition: Patch processing is the ability of convolutional layers to process small, localized sections of the input data. This capability builds in explicit parallelism into the computation.

concepts.name: Filter bank
concepts.definition: Filter bank is a set of different output convolutions that are learned in parallel when a convolutional layer needs to produce multiple channels of output. Instead of learning a single linear layer, the filter bank allows the network to build multiple independent output dimensions from the same data

concepts.name: Multi-channel inputs
concepts.definition: Multi-channel inputs refer to data that has depth, such as color images (like RGB), meaning the input is not just a spatial extent but a tensor with multiple channels. When performing convolution on these inputs, a different set of weights is learned for each input channel.

concepts.name: Feature channel
concepts.definition: Feature channel is one of the dimensions of the output of a convolutional layer, representing a specific feature map generated by a filter. The number of feature channels corresponds to the number of filters used in the convolutional layer.

concepts.name: Spatial extent
concepts.definition: Spatial extent refers to the dimensions of the filter, such as 3 by 3. This is the convention used when discussing filter size, focusing only on the spatial dimensions rather than the channel dimensions.

concepts.name: Feature map
concepts.definition: Feature map is an image that serves as a structural representation of the input data. It has height and width and is generated by applying a filter to the input.

concepts.name: Feature bank
concepts.definition: Feature bank is the collection of learned output channels that a convolutional layer produces. This bank shows what different filters activate when the input image is processed.

concepts.name: Feature collapse
concepts.definition: Feature collapse is a phenomenon where some features are ignored by the model. This can occur depending on the data, architecture, and optimization process.

concepts.name: Pooling
concepts.definition: Pooling is a function applied to a local patch that is essentially the same as running a convolutional layer without learning weights. This function uses predefined operations, such as the maximum or average function, to constrain the layer.

concepts.name: Downsampling
concepts.definition: Downsampling is a method used in neural networks, particularly for classification, where the high-dimensional input structure is intentionally reduced. This is done when the network does not require the full dimensional structure at every layer.

concepts.name: Strided operation
concepts.definition: Strided operation is a method that combines convolution or pooling with downsampling into a single element. It achieves this by increasing the stride of the filter, causing it to move further than a single pixel at each step.

concepts.name: Dilated filter
concepts.definition: Dilated filter is a type of filter where certain values are set to zero, which is baked into the model. This configuration allows the filter to capture information from a larger spatial context or extent while using fewer parameters.

concepts.name: Neural architecture search
concepts.definition: Neural architecture search is a field of research that specifically attempts to optimize over the vast space of possible architectures. This process aims to find the best possible solution for a given task.

concepts.name: Feature activations
concepts.definition: Feature activations are the outputs of a layer that represent complex information collected from the input image. These activations can become more semantically meaningful as they pass through multiple layers of the network.

concepts.name: Encoder-decoder architecture
concepts.definition: Encoder-decoder architecture is a structure that processes an input by first using convolution and downsampling to create a low-dimensional representation, and then uses convolution and upsampling to reconstruct the output.

concepts.name: U-net
concepts.definition: U-net is an architecture designed to bridge the gap between preserving high-resolution structure and maintaining computational efficiency, making it suitable for image-to-image tasks.

concepts.name: Skip connection
concepts.definition: Skip connection is a connection across different parts of an architecture that allows information to bypass intermediate layers and pass directly toward the output. This mechanism ensures the model does not have to force fine-grained spatial detail into a low-rank embedding.

concepts.name: ResNet architecture
concepts.definition: ResNet architecture is a deep learning model that utilizes a skipped connection in every single layer. This design allows the model to implicitly learn the optimal depth required for a specific task.

concepts.name: Residual connection
concepts.definition: Residual connection is a specific type of connection where the output of a layer is calculated by adding the layer's function output to the input dimension itself. This connection assumes that the output and the residual connection are the same size.

concepts.name: Convolutions in time
concepts.definition: Convolutions in time involve performing convolutions over a temporal dimension, allowing the model to build representations using time as one of the dimensions.

concepts.name: 3D convolutions
concepts.definition: 3D convolutions are a type of convolution that operates over both spatial dimensions and a temporal dimension, resulting in a lower dimensional representation.

concepts.name: Shift invariant in time
concepts.definition: Shift invariant in time is a property where the model's output remains the same regardless of when an event occurs within the temporal sequence.

concepts.name: Positional encoding
concepts.definition: Positional encoding is a method of adding location information to the input of convolutional filters. Positional encoding is constructed separately and added to the input signal, allowing the network to incorporate positional data into the convolution.

concepts.name: Neural field
concepts.definition: Neural field is a field that is parameterized fully or in part by a neural network. This allows the network to model a functional mapping from a coordinate grid, such as a position in an image, to an output value like color.

concepts.name: Neural Radiance Field
concepts.definition: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) is a popular architecture that applies a convolutional network to a map. NeRF takes a five-dimensional coordinate grid, which includes position and camera direction, as input and outputs color and volumetric density.

concepts.name: Strided convolution
concepts.definition: Strided convolution is a method that explicitly performs both pooling and downsampling simultaneously. This technique combines two operations into a single convolutional layer.

concepts.name: Fast and slow
concepts.definition: Fast and slow is a two-pronged approach for video processing where a low-dimensional subsampling model runs frequently to capture motion, while a secondary high-resolution channel periodically processes frames to capture fine-grained semantic details.

concepts.name: Graph neural network
concepts.definition: Graph neural networks are a class of architectures that generalize convolutional networks and are designed to be applied to specific types of problems.

concepts.name: Approximation power
concepts.definition: Approximation power refers to the capacity of a neural network to represent different types of functions. It also addresses the degree to which an architecture is universal.

concepts.name: Constraints
concepts.definition: Constraints are limitations added to a function approximator to rule out certain types of functions. This design choice allows the system to fit data only in specific, desired ways.

concepts.name: Transformer
concepts.definition: Transformer is the name given to a system where the aggregation operator is attention. This system utilizes attention to aggregate information across the graph structure.

concepts.name: Graph nets
concepts.definition: Graph nets are a general class of models designed to process information across graph structures. Transformers are a specific type of graph net that utilizes attention as its aggregation operator.

concepts.name: Node classification problem
concepts.definition: Node classification problem is a task where a question is asked about a specific node within a graph. This involves predicting a property or category for that individual node, such as whether a person likes a certain type of music.

concepts.name: Graph prediction problem
concepts.definition: Graph prediction problem involves asking a question about the entire graph structure, such as a molecule. This type of problem aims to predict properties based on the overall arrangement of atoms and bonds.

concepts.name: Probabilistic graphical model
concepts.definition: Probabilistic graphical model is a classical idea for representing probability distributions using a graph structure. Graph nets are appropriate for representing things like these distributions.

concepts.name: Discrete optimization
concepts.definition: Discrete optimization is a type of problem where decision variables are being optimized. The goal is to find a setting for these variables that satisfies a system of constraints.

concepts.name: Node embedding
concepts.definition: Node embedding is a vector that is learned specifically for each individual node within a graph. This vector provides information of interest about that particular node.

concepts.name: Graph embedding
concepts.definition: Graph embedding is a single vector that is learned to represent the entire graph. This vector allows for questions to be asked about the properties of the whole graph.

concepts.name: Attribute vector
concepts.definition: Attribute vector is the observed data associated with a single node in the graph. This vector provides specific information about that node.

concepts.name: Adjacency matrix
concepts.definition: Adjacency matrix is a representation used to describe the edges between nodes in a graph. This matrix serves as an additional input to the graph neural network.

concepts.name: Permutation invariance
concepts.definition: Permutation-invariant describes a function whose output remains the same even if the input items are reordered. This property ensures that the order in which neighbors are indexed does not affect the resulting message.

concepts.name: Permutation equivariance
concepts.definition: Permutation equivariance is a property where if the input data is permuted (reindexed), the output predictions are permuted in the exact same way. This ensures that shuffling the nodes results in a corresponding shuffle of the predictions.

concepts.name: Permutation matrix
concepts.definition: Permutation matrix is a matrix used to reorder the rows and columns of another matrix. Applying this matrix changes the indexing of the nodes without changing the underlying structure of the graph.

concepts.name: Local operation
concepts.definition: Local operation is a mechanism where data representation is updated by running local filters or computations. Every node in the graph receives input only from its immediate neighbors.

concepts.name: Aggregate function
concepts.definition: Aggregate function is a mechanism used to combine information from a node's neighbors into a single representation. This function must be permutation-invariant, meaning the order in which the neighbor information is processed does not affect the final result.

concepts.name: Update function
concepts.definition: Update function is a process that modifies a node's vector representation. It combines the information received from neighbors (messages) with the node's existing self-knowledge to refine its representation.

concepts.name: Multiset function
concepts.definition: Multiset function is the technical name for a function that takes a set of items, which may contain duplicates, and maps them to a vector. This concept is used when the input node vectors might not be unique.

concepts.name: Readout
concepts.definition: Readout is the final step in a graph network that converts the set of individual node embeddings into a single vector embedding for the entire graph. This process is essentially another multiset function applied over all nodes.

concepts.name: Message passing
concepts.definition: Message passing is the process of unrolling message passing iterations where every step updates a set of node vectors by taking input data and combining information from neighboring nodes. This process is the forward pass through the network.

concepts.name: Aggregate
concepts.definition: Aggregate is the function that takes all node vectors from a node's neighbors and combines them into a single D-dimensional vector. This combined vector serves as the message passed to the central node.

concepts.name: Update
concepts.definition: Update is the function that combines a node's existing embedding with the aggregated message from its neighbors. This operation applies a node-wise, vector-to-vector mapping to generate the node's updated representation.

concepts.name: Aggregation operation
concepts.definition: Aggregation operation is the function used to combine messages received from a node's neighbors. While simple methods like summing or averaging are possible, advanced variations include attention, which is a summation dependent on the value of the node embeddings.

concepts.name: Weight sharing idea
concepts.definition: Weight sharing idea means that all the aggregate functions used in parallel across all operations within one layer of the message-passing algorithm are the same function. This allows the model to generalize across graphs of different sizes.

concepts.name: Equivalence class
concepts.definition: Equivalence class is a set of graphs that a graph net cannot distinguish from one another. If two graphs belong to the same equivalence class, the graph net must assign the same prediction to both.

concepts.name: Tree structure
concepts.definition: Tree structure is the local neighborhood pattern that a node observes when updating its representation based on incoming messages. This structure forms the entire characterization of the graph from the perspective of a graph net.

concepts.name: Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm
concepts.definition: Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm is a classical graph theory algorithm that takes two graphs and decides whether they are structurally the same or different. The power of a graph net to distinguish graphs is limited by the capabilities of this algorithm.

concepts.name: Empirical risk
concepts.definition: Empirical risk is the average loss incurred over all of the available training data points. This measure quantifies how well a model fits the specific data it was trained on.

concepts.name: Population risk
concepts.definition: Population risk is the expected error when making predictions on new samples drawn from the entire data generating process. This represents how well the model performs in the real world.

concepts.name: Empirical test risk
concepts.definition: Empirical test risk is the measure of performance calculated over a finite sample, such as a designated test set. Population risk, conversely, is defined over the entire population of observations from the data generating process.

concepts.name: Generalization error
concepts.definition: Generalization error is the difference between the training error and the test error, or the training error and the population error.

concepts.name: Memorization
concepts.definition: Memorization is the process of determining what a model predicts specifically on the training data points. Generalization, in contrast, concerns how the model performs on data points where no training data was provided.

concepts.name: Filing cabinet
concepts.definition: Filing cabinet is a simple model type that memorizes training data by predicting specific values only for the points it has seen. For all other points, the filing cabinet predicts zero.

concepts.name: Large Language Model
concepts.definition: Large Language Model (LLM) is a family of advanced deep nets, such as ChatGPT, that are capable of complex prediction tasks. These models are used to process sequences of words as input and generate predictions.

concepts.name: Out-of-distribution input
concepts.definition: Out-of-distribution input refers to data that is systematically different from the data the model was trained on. These inputs are outside the scope of the training population.

concepts.name: Compositionality
concepts.definition: Compositionality is the property of an architecture that factors an input signal into small components, allowing the model to learn about each component individually while having the final conjunction of those components determined solely by the architecture's design, not by learned weights.

concepts.name: Occam's razor
concepts.definition: Occam's razor is a principle stating that among competing explanations that fit the data equally well, one should prefer the simplest model. This principle suggests that the simplest model that fits the data is most likely to generalize the best.

concepts.name: Shortest program
concepts.definition: The shortest program is a concept from algorithmic information theory that serves as a rigorous version of Occam's razor. This program is the one that perfectly fits or generates the data and is predicted to generalize best.

concepts.name: Bias
concepts.definition: Bias is defined as the training error. The bias is one component of the bias-variance trade-off, which relates the total test error to the training error and the variance.

concepts.name: Variance
concepts.definition: Variance is defined as the difference between the test error and the training error.

concepts.name: Double descent
concepts.definition: Double descent is a phenomenon where the generalization error of a model starts to improve again after initially worsening as the number of parameters increases. This suggests that the classical picture of overfitting is inaccurate.

concepts.name: Model capacity
concepts.definition: Model capacity is the complexity of a hypothesis space, which is classically measured by the number of parameters. Having too many parameters can lead to the model overfitting the training data.

concepts.name: Interpolation threshold
concepts.definition: Interpolation threshold is the point, as model capacity increases, at which the model can perfectly memorize all the training data. This threshold marks a critical point in the double descent phenomenon, where the model transitions from fitting the data to potentially generalizing better.

concepts.name: VC dimension
concepts.definition: VC dimension is a measure of capacity that counts the number of unique dichotomies a function class can apply to the training data. A higher VC dimension means the model can classify the training data in more different ways.

concepts.name: Dichotomy
concepts.definition: Dichotomy is a binary labeling of all the training data points, assigning each point to either a positive or negative class. This labeling is represented as a vector of assignments to positive one or negative one.

concepts.name: VC theory (Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory)
concepts.definition: VC theory is a framework that relates the size of the training data to the number of distinct functions in the hypothesis space. This theory provides a guarantee that population error matches training error if the data size is sufficiently large relative to the hypothesis space size.

concepts.name: Version space
concepts.definition: The version space is the set of all hypotheses within the hypothesis space that perfectly fit the given training data. In neural networks, this is the set of all parameter settings that achieve zero training error.

concepts.name: Parameter function map
concepts.definition: The parameter function map is the relationship that connects the parameters (weights and biases) of a model to the actual mathematical function that the model defines. This map is many-to-one, meaning multiple parameter vectors can define the same function.

concepts.name: Simplicity bias
concepts.definition: Simplicity bias is the empirical observation that when parameters are randomly sampled in a neural network, the resulting functions tend to be simple according to complexity measures like Lempel-Ziv complexity. This means that most random settings of weights and biases map to functions that are compressible, rather than complex or uncompressible.

concepts.name: Kernel matrix
concepts.definition: Kernel matrix is a matrix that characterizes the representation of input data at the output of a neural network. Every row and column in this matrix represents a data point, and the value indicates the similarity between those two data points in the network's representational vectors.

concepts.name: Rank
concepts.definition: Rank is a measure of a matrix indicating the number of linearly independent rows and columns it contains. Blockier matrices, which indicate clustered data, tend to have a lower rank, suggesting a simpler data format.

concepts.name: Effective rank
concepts.definition: Effective rank is a variation of the matrix rank used to characterize the representation of data. Lower effective rank signifies a more clustered-like structure in the data representation.

concepts.name: Weight decay
concepts.definition: Weight decay is a type of explicit regularizer used in optimization. It works by tending to shrink the weights during each update step, which helps the network learn simpler solutions.

concepts.name: Flat minima
concepts.definition: Flat minima are basins in the objective function's energy landscape where the loss is low over a large region of the parameter space. These flat minima are argued to generalize better than narrow minima.

concepts.name: Invariance
concepts.definition: Invariance is a property where a model's output remains unchanged despite a transformation of the input, such as when a max pooling operation is applied over channels. This allows the model to be insensitive to specific input orientations.

concepts.name: Equivariance
concepts.definition: Equivariance is a property where a transformation applied to the input causes a corresponding, predictable transformation in the model's predictions. For instance, if the input nodes are permuted, the predictions will also be permuted.

concepts.name: Domain knowledge
concepts.definition: Domain knowledge is specialized information, such as equations of perspective projection or light transport, that is intentionally built into a neural architecture. This allows the model to generalize by using inherent structures rather than merely fitting the training data.

concepts.name: Optimization
concepts.definition: Optimization is the remaining core question in deep learning, distinct from approximation and generalization, which are argued to be solved by simply using large models and massive datasets. Optimization focuses on making the training process as efficient as possible when deploying big neural networks.

concepts.name: Neural network
concepts.definition: Neural network is a function that takes inputs and weights and produces an output. This function is the core component of the model being trained.

concepts.name: Loss function
concepts.definition: Loss function is a classic machine learning function that measures the discrepancy between the neural network's output and the target value across the dataset. This function is typically averaged over all the training data points.

concepts.name: Learning rate
concepts.definition: Learning rate is the step size, denoted as eta, which determines how large the steps are when moving the weights during the gradient descent operation.

concepts.name: Scaling
concepts.definition: Scaling refers to increasing the size of a neural network, which can be achieved by making the network wider or by making the network deeper. This process is done to improve the overall performance of the network.

concepts.name: Scaling the width
concepts.definition: Scaling the width involves making the neural network wider, which is one method of increasing network size. This scaling generally leads to a better achieved loss, improving performance.

concepts.name: First order methods
concepts.definition: First order methods are optimization algorithms that rely exclusively on using the first derivatives of the loss function. These methods are the type of approach commonly used in deep learning.

concepts.name: Second order methods
concepts.definition: Second order methods are optimization algorithms that utilize both first derivatives and second derivatives of the loss function. These methods incorporate a big matrix of second derivatives, in addition to the standard gradients.

concepts.name: Gradient
concepts.definition: The gradient is the derivative of the loss with respect to the weights, which is the quantity obtained by performing back propagation. It is conceptually treated as one large vector.

concepts.name: Hessian
concepts.definition: Hessian matrix is a $d \times d$ matrix that represents the second-order term in the Taylor expansion of the loss function, where $d$ is the number of parameters in the neural network.

concepts.name: Newton's method
concepts.definition: Newton's method is an optimization algorithm that uses both first and second-order information to determine an optimization step. It is described as preconditioning the gradient with the inverse Hessian.

concepts.name: Linearization of our loss function
concepts.definition: Linearization of our loss function refers to the first-order term of the Taylor expansion. This term is defined as the gradient inner product delta w.

concepts.name: Quadratic form
concepts.definition: Quadratic form is the structure that the Taylor expansion takes when calculated up to the second order, incorporating both the first-order gradient term and the second-order Hessian term. This form is subsequently minimized with respect to the weight perturbation $\delta w$ to determine the optimization step.

concepts.name: Gauss-Newton decomposition
concepts.definition: Gauss-Newton decomposition is a formula derived for the second derivative of a composite objective function. This decomposition splits the full Hessian into two pieces based on the product rule.

concepts.name: Composite objective function
concepts.definition: A composite objective function is a function that is the composition of two other functions. This structure is common in machine learning, such as when combining an error function and a neural network.

concepts.name: Gauss-Newton method
concepts.definition: Gauss-Newton method is an iterative weight update algorithm derived from the Gauss-Newton decomposition. This method approximates the full Hessian by making assumptions—such as using squared error and ignoring model curvature—which simplifies the Hessian into a product of derivatives.

concepts.name: Forward mode automatic differentiation
concepts.definition: Forward mode automatic differentiation is a technique used for calculating derivatives, which is noted to be significantly more computationally expensive than backpropagation.

concepts.name: Steepest descent
concepts.definition: Steepest descent is an optimization algorithm that decomposes movement into a step size and a step direction. Under a Euclidean norm penalty, the step direction is chosen to point exactly in the direction of the gradient.

concepts.name: Infinity norm
concepts.definition: The infinity norm is a measure that determines the maximum size of a vector across all its coordinates. When using this norm, the unit ball takes on the shape of a square.

concepts.name: Singular Value Decomposition
concepts.definition: Singular Value Decomposition is a generalized eigenvalue decomposition that every matrix possesses. This decomposition allows one to mentally break down each weight matrix in a neural network.

concepts.name: Steepest descent problem
concepts.definition: Steepest descent problem is an optimization problem whose solution can be separated into two distinct parts: computing the step size and computing the direction.

concepts.name: Non-isotropic space
concepts.definition: Non-isotropic space is a mathematical space where the axes are not equal to each other, meaning that different directions have different scales or magnitudes. This condition arises when the loss function does not have the property that all directions in the weight space are equal.

concepts.name: Matrix norm
concepts.definition: Matrix norm is a mathematical tool used to measure the size or scale of a matrix. It allows researchers to quantify whether a weight update is too big or too small.

concepts.name: Spectral norm
concepts.definition: Spectral norm is a type of matrix norm defined as the largest singular value of a matrix.

concepts.name: Induced operator norm
concepts.definition: Induced operator norm is a method for defining a norm on a matrix by specifying arbitrary norms for both the input and output vector spaces. This allows the measurement of a matrix's size to be tailored to the specific norms used for the activations within a neural network layer.

concepts.name: RMS to RMS operator norm
concepts.definition: RMS to RMS operator norm is the induced operator norm applied to a matrix when both the input and output vector spaces are equipped with the RMS norm. This norm measures the maximum RMS norm of the output given a unit RMS norm input.

concepts.name: Operator norm
concepts.definition: Operator norm is a mathematical measure that provides an upper-bound on how much the features of a particular layer can change. This norm does not guarantee that the features will change by this amount, only that they cannot change more than this amount.

concepts.name: Width scaling problem
concepts.definition: Width scaling problem is the issue of removing drift in the optimal learning rate as the width of a neural network is varied. Defining and utilizing a particular norm for normalization is the proposed solution to this problem.

concepts.name: Expressivity
concepts.definition: Expressivity is the capacity of the neural network to approximate functions, and the goal is to constrain network properties without damaging this approximation capacity.

concepts.name: Well-scaled depth limit
concepts.definition: Well-scaled depth limit is a condition where a compound system, composed of many terms, remains stable when the number of terms approaches infinity. This stability is achieved by carefully scaling the internals of the system.

concepts.name: Block multiplier
concepts.definition: Block multiplier is a factor placed in front of blocks within a residual network. This factor is crucial for ensuring that the network's dynamics do not blow up or go to zero as the depth increases.

concepts.name: Module
concepts.definition: A module is an abstraction that handles inputs in an input space, outputs in an output space, and possesses weights in a weight space. Modules can represent either an individual layer or a full neural network.

concepts.name: Atomic module
concepts.definition: An atomic module is one of the basic layer types that forms the library, such as ReLU, linear, convolution, or embedding. These modules are the fundamental building blocks of the network.

concepts.name: Forward function
concepts.definition: A forward function is the function that the module expresses, which represents the primary operation of the module. This function dictates how the module processes its inputs.

concepts.name: Backward function
concepts.definition: A backward function is the derivatives of the forward function. This function is necessary for computing the derivatives during optimization.

concepts.name: Transformer
concepts.definition: Transformer is an architecture that operates over tokens, representing a single concrete instantiation rather than the general class of functions and parameterizations discussed in graph nets.

concepts.name: Attention
concepts.definition: Attention is a mechanism that determines how a linear combination is performed between tokens, where the weights used are not fixed parameters but are derived from activations elsewhere in the network.

concepts.name: Token
concepts.definition: Token is an encapsulated unit of operations that serves as the fundamental unit in the architecture. It is a vector-valued unit, which distinguishes it from a scalar-valued neuron.

concepts.name: Locality bias
concepts.definition: Locality bias is the inherent characteristic of CNNs that forces them to factorize the signal processing problem into small, local pieces.

concepts.name: Fully connected network
concepts.definition: Fully connected network is a type of neural network where every single output neuron is connected to every input neuron. This structure allows information to be aggregated immediately and globally across the entire input.

concepts.name: Sparsely globally
concepts.definition: Sparsely globally is an approach that allows a network to look at the entire input signal without requiring every neuron to be connected to every other neuron. This method maintains a global view while significantly reducing the computational load and number of parameters.

concepts.name: Set of tokens
concepts.definition: Set of tokens is the primary data structure used to represent information in the transformer model. This set consists of multiple tokens, which are the basic units over which the transformer operates.

concepts.name: Tokenization
concepts.definition: Tokenization is the general strategy where a domain expert converts raw data into discrete tokens that the generic transformer can process. Tokenization allows the transformer to operate on chunks of data that make sense within the specific domain.

concepts.name: Byte pair
concepts.definition: Byte pairs are a tokenization method that represents words using pairs of characters. These tokens are frequently used even in the largest scale language models.

concepts.name: Linear combination operation
concepts.definition: Linear combination operation is a generalization of the linear combination performed over individual neurons, allowing the combination of entire token vectors using learned weights.

concepts.name: Linear combination of tokens
concepts.definition: Linear combination of tokens is a weighted combination of token vectors, represented by multiplying a weight vector $w$ by the token matrix $T$. This operation is less expressive than a standard neuron linear combination because the number of weights is limited by the number of tokens, resulting in a low-rank transformation over the individual neurons.

concepts.name: Low rank transformation
concepts.definition: Low rank transformation is a mathematical operation where the number of weights determining the combination is significantly smaller than the total number of individual neurons that make up the tokens. This makes the token linear combination a less expressive family of layers.

concepts.name: Token-wise nonlinearity
concepts.definition: Token-wise nonlinearity is a function that operates on each token independently and identically. This nonlinearity passes every token in the array through the same nonlinear function F.

concepts.name: Token net
concepts.definition: Token net is an architecture that performs a linear combination of tokens. This process involves taking a weighted sum of tokens, followed by a token-wise nonlinearity.

concepts.name: Linear combination
concepts.definition: Linear combination is a mathematical operation where the output is calculated as a weighted sum of input tokens, which is the basis for how tokens are combined into a new representation.

concepts.name: Unrolled GNN (Graph Neural Network)
concepts.definition: Unrolled GNN (Graph Neural Network) is a network structure that utilizes an aggregate function for weighted combination, followed by a combined unit-wise nonlinearity, and repeats this process. Unrolled GNNs often possess the property of sharing weights across depth, though this is an optional design choice.

concepts.name: Weight matrix
concepts.definition: Weight matrix is a matrix containing free parameters that determines the coefficients used in a linear combination, which are learnable via backpropagation, unlike the data-dependent weights used in attention mechanisms.

concepts.name: Query
concepts.definition: Query is a special operation that emits a vector based on the contents of the question's embedding vector. This vector is used to determine which parts of the input signal the model should attend to.

concepts.name: Query-key-value attention
concepts.definition: Query-key-value attention is the mathematical formulation of the most common kind of attention, which allows the transformer to map from a set of input tokens to a set of output tokens. This mechanism involves using a query to determine relevance against keys and then aggregating values.

concepts.name: Key
concepts.definition: Key is a function associated with each token that emits a vector, which the query attempts to match against. This vector represents the content of the token that the query should match to.

concepts.name: Value
concepts.definition: Value is an operation that transforms a token vector into the information that will be reported to the next layer of the network. This vector contains the actual content that is retrieved when a query matches a key.

concepts.name: Dot product
concepts.definition: Dot product between the key vector and the query vector measures how relevant a specific key is to a specific query. This operation functions as a way of measuring the similarity between the two vectors.

concepts.name: Attention layer
concepts.definition: Attention layer is a concrete mechanism that utilizes three learnable matrices to transform a token vector into query, key, and value vectors. These projections constitute the learnable parameters of the attention layer.

concepts.name: Learnable parameters
concepts.definition: Learnable parameters are the matrices that the model learns during training, such as the matrices that transform a token vector into a query, key, or value. These parameters are essential components of the attention layer.

concepts.name: Query vector
concepts.definition: Query vector is a linear projection of the token vector, which is used to determine the relevance of other tokens. The query function maps from the question vector, which is represented by a token vector.

concepts.name: Key vector
concepts.definition: Key vector is a linear projection of the token vector, which is used to be compared against a query vector. This comparison measures the similarity between the key and the query.

concepts.name: Self-attention
concepts.definition: Self-attention is an idea where the weights used in a linear combination are determined as a function of the input sequence itself. This allows the model to weigh the importance of different tokens relative to each other.

concepts.name: Value vector
concepts.definition: Value vector is a vector emitted by every token in the input sequence via a projection (WV) that holds the actual information being combined in the linear combination. The attention mechanism weights these vectors to form the output.

concepts.name: Attention equation
concepts.definition: Attention equation is the mathematical condensation of the self-attention process, which involves multiplying the query matrix by the transpose of the key matrix. This operation calculates the similarity between all pairs of queries and keys.

concepts.name: Convolution
concepts.definition: Convolution is a computational operation that uses a much lower rank matrix compared to a fully connected layer. This structure allows for far fewer learnable parameters while maintaining translation equivariance.

concepts.name: Low rank
concepts.definition: Low rank describes a matrix that can be represented using fewer parameters than its full dimensions would suggest. This property is advantageous because it reduces the number of linear learnable parameters in the model.

concepts.name: Set-to-set mapping
concepts.definition: Set-to-set mapping is a function where an unordered set of inputs maps to an unordered set of outputs. This characteristic implies that the ordering of the tokens does not inherently matter for the transformation.

concepts.name: Autoregressive model
concepts.definition: Autoregressive model predicts the next word in a sequence by taking the previous prediction and appending it to the input sequence, then continuing the process. This model is trained to ensure its predictions match the actual text observed in the training set.

concepts.name: Causal attention
concepts.definition: Causal attention is a mechanism where the prediction of a token depends only on the preceding tokens in the sequence. This ensures a causal dependency, meaning a word only depends on the previous words.

concepts.name: Autoregressive transformer
concepts.definition: Autoregressive transformer is a type of transformer that generates output sequentially by predicting the next item in a sequence based on previously generated items. The process involves predicting the next item, shifting the input, and repeating the cycle.

concepts.name: Causal masking
concepts.definition: Causal masking is a technique applied to the attention matrix that ensures every output token can only attend to tokens that appeared earlier in the sequence. This operation prevents the model from looking into the future, which is necessary for generating text in time's order.

concepts.name: Feedforward
concepts.definition: Feedforward is the token-wise nonlinearity that involves applying a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) independently and identically to every single token vector.

concepts.name: Autoregressive part
concepts.definition: Autoregressive part is a component of the model related to autoregressive modeling, where the prediction process generates outputs sequentially based on previous steps.

concepts.name: Cross-attention
concepts.definition: Cross-attention is a mechanism where a set of tokens attends to a different, separate set of tokens, such as text tokens attending to image tokens.

concepts.name: Hacks
concepts.definition: Hacks are practical tips and methods that have historically driven progress in deep learning. These are often anecdotal insights from practitioners rather than formal mathematical theory.

concepts.name: Generalization bounds
concepts.definition: Generalization bounds are theoretical limits derived from classical theories that predict how well a system will perform. These bounds can be rendered vacuous when dealing with deep nets.

concepts.name: Spurious correlation
concepts.definition: Spurious correlation is a shortcut where a deep net uses an irrelevant feature, such as a marker in the corner of an image, instead of the actual tissue to make a classification.

concepts.name: Bias in the data
concepts.definition: Bias in the data occurs when the training data itself contains a systematic skew, such as only including malignant tumors from a specific hospital, which gives away the answer.

concepts.name: Imbalanced data set
concepts.definition: Imbalanced data set is a common failure scenario where the training data contains significantly more examples of one class than another, such as having 99% of cases being non-cancerous.

concepts.name: Reinforcement learning
concepts.definition: Reinforcement learning is a fundamental concept involving an iterative loop where an agent first searches for high-scoring action sequences, and then fits a neural network (a policy) to directly map from the state to the optimal action. This process is repeated, guiding the search toward better actions until maximal reward is achieved under certain conditions.

concepts.name: Loss curve
concepts.definition: Loss curve is a visual representation of training progress that shows how the model's loss changes over time during an experiment.

concepts.name: Imbalanced set of target outputs
concepts.definition: An imbalanced set of target outputs occurs when the training data contains a disproportionate number of one class compared to others. This imbalance can lead to trivial performance metrics if the model simply guesses the majority class.

concepts.name: Data preprocessing
concepts.definition: Data preprocessing is the necessary step of preparing raw data into the specific format required for the model to process it correctly. Failure to preprocess data can lead to significant bugs, such as incorrect range assumptions.

concepts.name: Requires gradient
concepts.definition: Requires gradient is a property that must be set to true for any parameter that needs to be trained, allowing the network to calculate gradients during training.

concepts.name: Shape
concepts.definition: Shape is the dimensional structure of tensors in deep learning, and this structure is considered super critical for the proper functioning of the network.

concepts.name: Data type
concepts.definition: Data type specifies the format of the data, such as whether it is a 32-bit tensor or a uint8, which is an important characteristic to inspect.

concepts.name: Standardization transformation
concepts.definition: Standardization transformation is a data normalization technique where the data is transformed by subtracting the mean and dividing by the square root of the variance. This process aims to remove dependence on the unit of measure and the scale of the data, resulting in a zero mean and unit variance distribution.

concepts.name: Layernorm (Layer Normalization)
concepts.definition: Layernorm (Layer normalization) is a normalization layer that requires sufficient layer dimensionality to function correctly. The instructor notes that it will not work well if the layer dimensionality is small.

concepts.name: High dimensions
