concepts.definition: High dimensions refer to spaces where the properties of data, such as a Gaussian distribution, differ significantly from human intuition derived from low-dimensional spaces. Things become simple in high dimensions, which is a key concept in deep learning.

concepts.name: Low dimensions
concepts.definition: Low dimensions refer to spaces, like the three spatial coordinates we experience, where human intuition is typically applied to understand objects and data. The lecture warns students to be careful when working in low dimensions.

concepts.name: Unit hypersphere
concepts.definition: Unit hypersphere is the geometric shape that RMS-norm tends to map data points onto, resulting in all data being normalized to the unit scale.

concepts.name: Batch norm (Batch normalization)
concepts.definition: Batch normalization is a technique that normalizes activations using the statistics derived from a specific data batch. This process introduces a strong dependency between the model's performance and the batch size.

concepts.name: Asymptotically
concepts.definition: Asymptotic analysis is a standard part of computer science that examines how a property of a model scales as resources, complexity, or an input parameter increases. This technique is used to predict how the model's behavior will scale in the future.

concepts.name: Uint8
concepts.definition: Uint8 is an unsigned 8-bit integer data type. Because it is unsigned, it cannot represent negative numbers, meaning any negative data will be lost or corrupted when stored in this format.

concepts.name: Standardization
concepts.definition: Standardization is a process where input data is transformed to be centered on zero and have a unit variance. This transformation allows the data to contain negative values.

concepts.name: Einops
concepts.definition: Einops is a library designed to simplify complex tensor manipulation by providing a common notation for operations like reshape, flatten, and unsqueeze. This library helps make keeping track of reshape operations easier for the user.

concepts.name: Rearrange
concepts.definition: Rearrange is a function within einops that uses a string notation to specify how a set of reshapes maps a tensor from one space to another space. This string acts as a shorthand for defining the required dimensional mapping.

concepts.name: Row contiguous
concepts.definition: Row contiguous describes the order in which a tensor is read when reshaping, meaning the operation processes the first row entirely before moving to the next row. This behavior dictates how the data is sequenced when dimensions are flattened.

concepts.name: Inverse operation
concepts.definition: An inverse operation is a sequence of operations that, when performed after an initial operation, returns the system to its original state. This property allows the original tensor to be recovered after a transformation.

concepts.name: Data augmentation
concepts.definition: Data augmentation is a technique that adds more data points to a dataset, which makes the learning problem more difficult for the model to solve.

concepts.name: Domain randomization
concepts.definition: Domain randomization is a method where random variation is added to the training environment to increase the difficulty of the problem, allowing the model to generalize better.

concepts.name: Robustness
concepts.definition: Robustness is the quality of a model that allows it to maintain performance even when facing variations or errors in the input data. By training with randomized inputs, the model becomes robust to potential miscalibrations or errors.

concepts.name: N-gram model
concepts.definition: N-gram model is a statistical model that represents how words co-occur with each other in a sequence. These models are used to estimate the probability of word sequences.

concepts.name: Joint distribution
concepts.definition: Joint distribution is the statistical measure that the N-gram error models, representing the probability of all elements occurring together. This distribution considers the entire sequence of words simultaneously.

concepts.name: Conditional distribution
concepts.definition: Conditional distribution is the statistical measure that the current model is designed to model, specifically the probability of the last word given the preceding words. This focuses on predicting the next element based on the input history.

concepts.name: Delta function
concepts.definition: Delta function is a mathematical representation of a single point, which occurs when the probability of an output becomes completely deterministic.

concepts.name: Regression
concepts.definition: Regression is a task where standard neural net training uses functions like L2 loss to take inputs and make a single point prediction of the output value.

concepts.name: Distribution shift
concepts.definition: Distribution shifts represent changes in the data distribution, which can be addressed either by aiming for generalizably robust performance against any hypothetical change, or by specializing and adapting to a specific, known distribution shift.

concepts.name: Data diversity and coverage
concepts.definition: Data diversity and coverage is the key factor that matters when dealing with rare classes of interest. This concept suggests that the data must adequately represent all the different things that are important in the domain.

concepts.name: Context
concepts.definition: Context is additional information added into the inputs of a model to provide surrounding circumstances. By knowing the context, a model can adjust its probability of certain states, such as reducing the probability of a crash if the context is an amusement park.

concepts.name: Pre-training
concepts.definition: Pre-training is the initial phase where a network is trained on a large amount of data to learn a general representation. This representation learning phase does not require specific knowledge about the final task.

concepts.name: Pre-trained model
concepts.definition: Pretrained model is a single, large model designed to handle multiple tasks. Unlike older methods that required collecting targeted data sets and training task-specific models, this model is trained on broad data so that it already contains the necessary information for many downstream tasks.

concepts.name: Out-of-domain data
concepts.definition: Out-of-domain data is data that is not specific to the problem being solved, and using it in the training set is beneficial because it helps put as much information into the model as possible.

concepts.name: State of the art model
concepts.definition: Segment Anything Model (SAM) is a modern segmentation model that relies on building a very large dataset. This model uses self-supervision and specific augmentation techniques to learn a generalizable and robust segmentation capability.

concepts.name: Empirical risk minimization
concepts.definition: Empirical risk minimization is a form of optimization where the risk function is minimized based on the training data. Empirical max likelihood is a specific instance of this, where the risk function is the likelihood of the data.

concepts.name: Quantize
concepts.definition: Quantize is the process of reducing a continuous space into discrete classes. This allows continuous values, such as colors, to be represented by distinct, countable categories.

concepts.name: Softmax regression
concepts.definition: Softmax regression is a standard machine learning technique where a function is learned to map input data, such as images, to a distribution over the probability of each class. This distribution indicates how much probability is placed on each possible class.

concepts.name: Softmax distribution
concepts.definition: Softmax distribution is a fully expressive categorical distribution that models a probability mass function over a discrete vocabulary. This distribution is the most general way of quantifying uncertainty over a discrete variable.

concepts.name: One-hot vector
concepts.definition: One-hot vector is a representation used to label discrete classes, similar to how labels are used in standard classification problems. Each class is represented by a vector where only one element is active.

concepts.name: Batch size
concepts.definition: Batch size is a cardinal hyperparameter in deep learning that dictates how many data points are processed simultaneously during training. Batch normalization introduces a strong dependency on this parameter, which can complicate model tuning.

concepts.name: Exponentially Moving Average
concepts.definition: Exponentially Moving Average is a technique used to smooth out values over time. This method mixes a new value with previous values, where the contribution of older values is exponentially decayed by a specific factor.

concepts.name: Sequence modeling
concepts.definition: Sequence modeling is the process of modeling data that possesses an inherent order or temporal structure, such as time or order. This approach allows models to handle information that unfolds over a series of steps.

concepts.name: Recurrent Neural Network
concepts.definition: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are a type of network developed to capture context by remembering information from the past of a sequence.

concepts.name: Long Short-Term Memory
concepts.definition: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is a specific subset of Recurrent Neural Networks. LSTMs are designed to specifically avoid the common issue of forgetting that is present in standard RNNs.

concepts.name: Autoregression
concepts.definition: Autoregressively, a model is trained to predict the next character in a sequence based on the characters that came before it. This method is used in models like GPT-3 to generate text sequentially.

concepts.name: Sequence
concepts.definition: Sequence is an ordered collection of data points that can represent various types of information. These sequences include words in language, pictures in a video, or audio signals.

concepts.name: Space-time cube
concepts.definition: Space-time cube is a four-dimensional tensor created by extending convolutional neural networks (CNNs) into the space-time dimension. This structure allows for the representation of data that includes spatial dimensions and a temporal dimension.

concepts.name: Memory unit
concepts.definition: Memory unit is a component that provides context by storing and giving information about what has been seen in the past of a sequence.

concepts.name: Hidden unit
concepts.definition: Hidden unit is a concept introduced in recurrent neural networks that allows the model to maintain an infinite context, unlike models that rely on a fixed window in time. This unit captures memory by taking the current temporal input and the previous hidden state and passing that information forward to the next time step.

concepts.name: Hidden state
concepts.definition: Hidden state is a component of the network designed to capture the most relevant historical information from previous inputs. This state allows the network to maintain a memory of past data points.

concepts.name: Recurrence
concepts.definition: Recurrence is the process where information is sent forward over time, allowing the network to process sequential data. This mechanism enables the network to depend on previous states to determine the current state.

concepts.name: Deep recurrent neural network
concepts.definition: Deep recurrent neural network is an architecture that stacks multiple hidden layers, allowing for many different hidden states to process sequential data. This structure extends the basic recurrent unit by adding depth.

concepts.name: Fixed time window
concepts.definition: Fixed time window is a predetermined duration during training that the model is configured to propagate back through. This window allows the recurrent network to be unrolled into a structure suitable for backpropagation.

concepts.name: Unroll
concepts.definition: Unroll is the process of expanding a recurrent network over a specific time window. This process transforms the network, which originally contained loops, into a directed acyclic graph.

concepts.name: Markov assumption
concepts.definition: Markov assumption dictates that the future hidden state depends solely on the immediate preceding hidden state. This constraint is what allows Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to be called recurrent, even though they theoretically model dependencies over long chains.

concepts.name: Recurrent
concepts.definition: Recurrent describes a model where the hidden state depends only on the immediate hidden state from the previous step. This structure allows the model to process sequences of data.

concepts.name: Activations
concepts.definition: Activation is fast memory that captures statistics or memory of an existing data point as it runs through the network. This memory represents a quick snapshot of the data being processed at any given time.

concepts.name: Cell state
concepts.definition: Cell state is a new component introduced in an LSTM that functions like the hidden tape in a Turing machine. This state is modulated by the mechanisms that decide what information to forget and what information to add.

concepts.name: Gating functionality
concepts.definition: Gating functionality is the mechanism provided by multiplicative updates to the cell state, allowing the model to explicitly learn what information to remember and what information to forget. This functionality is provided by components that decide what to save and what to delete.

concepts.name: Sigmoid function
concepts.definition: Sigmoid function is a non-linearity used in the LSTM that is bounded between 0 and 1. This bounding allows the function to map large values to 1 and small values to 0.

concepts.name: Identity
concepts.definition: Identity is the default behavior of the LSTM, which is similar to a skipped or residual connection in a ResNet. This allows the model to potentially learn to simply send the same information forward without modification.

concepts.name: Softmax
concepts.definition: Softmax is a function that takes an input and transforms it into a probability distribution. This function ensures that the outputs are non-negative and sum up to one.

concepts.name: Next-word classifier
concepts.definition: Next-word classifier is a model designed to predict the most likely word that follows a given sequence of words. This model treats the sequence prediction task as a multi-class classification problem.

concepts.name: Teacher forcing
concepts.definition: Teacher forcing is a training technique where the model is conditioned on the ground-truth preceding words, even if the model predicts an incorrect word at a given time step. This prevents the model from penalizing itself for mistakes made after the initial error.

concepts.name: Beam search
concepts.definition: Beam search is a decoding technique that allows the model to choose the top k most likely candidates at each step. It fills out a tree of possibilities and selects the path that scores best overall, representing the model's confidence in the entire sequence.

concepts.name: Attention
concepts.definition: Attention is a mechanism where weights are dynamically determined as a function of the data, which makes the way information is kept dependent on the inputs. This flexibility allows for highly adaptable sequence modeling.

concepts.name: Convolution
concepts.definition: Convolution is a method for modeling arbitrarily long sequences using a fixed set of convolution weights that are shared over time. However, this method cannot see anything outside of the defined time window of that convolution.

concepts.name: Self-attention
concepts.definition: Self-attention is a computation where the similarity of the entire sequence is calculated against itself. This process requires an $N^2$ computation, where $N$ is the length of the sequence.

concepts.name: Retrieval enhanced transformers
concepts.definition: Retrieval enhanced transformers is an architecture that decomposes a large language model into a lightweight language model and a memory bank. This setup allows the model to perform fact lookup in a database, helping to enforce factual validity.

concepts.name: Context window
concepts.definition: Context window is the maximum number of tokens or data points that a model can consider or process at one time. This limit determines how far back in the input sequence a model can look when generating output.

concepts.name: Minimum certificate set
concepts.definition: Minimum certificate set is the smallest total amount of frames or clips of a video that is required to accurately recognize a specific action. This concept helps determine the necessary temporal scope for a task.

concepts.name: Representation
concepts.definition: Representation is the transformed version of data that is produced by a neural network. Each layer within the deep net holds a representation of the input data.

concepts.name: Encoding direction
concepts.definition: Encoding direction is the forward process through a neural network. This direction transforms raw data into simpler, more abstract representations.

concepts.name: Clustering
concepts.definition: Clustering is the problem of taking data and assigning each data point to a specific cluster. From a representation-learning perspective, clustering involves learning an encoder that outputs an integer representing the cluster assignment.

concepts.name: Self-supervised learning
concepts.definition: Self-supervised learning is a method of learning representations where the input data is not provided as paired input-output examples. Instead, the system learns a good representation from the input data (x) alone, without an explicit target.

concepts.name: Data to vector (X2vec)
concepts.definition: Data to vector (X2vec) is an idea for transforming input data (X) into vector representations. This technique has been developed for all different modalities, such as words or images, with word2vec being a famous early version.

concepts.name: Encoder
concepts.definition: Encoder is a function that maps data from a specific domain or distribution into vector embeddings in R^d. This function assigns a feature vector to every element in the input domain.

concepts.name: Softmax
concepts.definition: Softmax is a function that maps input data to a point within the simplex. The output of Softmax represents the probability of belonging to different classes.

concepts.name: Simplex
concepts.definition: Simplex is the set of points in R^d where the dimensions of those points sum up to 1. The output of a Softmax function is always a point in the simplex.

concepts.name: L2 norm
concepts.definition: L2 norm is a function that takes all data and maps it to unitary vectors. Unitary vectors are vectors that possess a norm of 1.

concepts.name: Binary classification
concepts.definition: Binary classification is a task where the goal is to categorize input data into one of two distinct classes. In this example, the task involves separating red points from blue points.

concepts.name: Non-linear classification problem
concepts.definition: A Non-linear classification problem is a scenario where no single linear hyperplane can successfully separate the different classes of data. This requires a more complex transformation to achieve separation.

concepts.name: Spectral descent method
concepts.definition: Spectral descent algorithm is a method that utilizes steepest descent specifically under the spectral norm. This algorithm is used to achieve faster training speeds in deep learning models.

concepts.name: Classification
concepts.definition: Classification is a task where a network is trained to find a way to disentangle different classes of data. The network's representation is separated in a high-dimensional space so that a final softmax operation can predict the correct class.

concepts.name: Mechanistic interpretability
concepts.definition: Mechanistic interpretability is a modern name for the type of work that involves probing and interpreting the representations learned within deep neural networks. This field seeks to understand what the emergent detectors are within these complex systems.

concepts.name: Pattern detector
concepts.definition: A pattern detector is a neuron or filter in a deep network that becomes selectively responsive to increasingly complex patterns as the network progresses through more layers. These detectors range from simple edges to complex objects like faces.

concepts.name: Learned representation
concepts.definition: Learned representation is the set of weights and biases that parameterize the encoder function. This set of parameters constitutes the learned representation of the data distribution.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning
concepts.definition: Fine-tuning is the process of taking a pre-trained model and further training it on a smaller, specialized dataset to adapt it for a particular application.

concepts.name: Autoencoder
concepts.definition: Autoencoder is a type of model that learns representations by compressing input data and then reconstructing the original input from the compressed form. The process results in a different representation of the data, rather than strictly a better one.

concepts.name: Minimal sufficient representation
concepts.definition: Minimal sufficient representation is a representation that is very low-dimensional or low-information, but still contains sufficient statistics for solving specific tasks. Minimal sufficient representation is informative toward the tasks of interest that the system is designed to care about.

concepts.name: Compact representation
concepts.definition: Compact representation is a representation that is small, allowing for the storage of low-dimensional features using less memory than the raw data itself. Compact representation also allows for simpler abstractions that generalize better, following an Occam's razor generalization theory.

concepts.name: Disentangled representation
concepts.definition: Disentangled representation is a representation that separates the interesting factors of variation within the data into independent dimensions. Disentangled representation is also referred to as an axis-aligned representation.

concepts.name: Interpretable representation
concepts.definition: Interpretable representation is a representation that allows a human to use it to solve problems and understand the underlying data. Interpretable representation is a consideration alongside other properties of a good representation.

concepts.name: Resilient representation
concepts.definition: Resilient representation is a representation that is robust and stable when the input data changes. Resilient representation prevents the representation from becoming fragile or going crazy when small amounts of noise are added to the data.

concepts.name: Embedding vector
concepts.definition: Embedding vector is a univariate function of the input data $x$, meaning it is a function of $x$ alone. This contrasts with a distance metric, which is a bivariate function of two data points, $x_1$ and $x_2$.

concepts.name: Compression
concepts.definition: Compression is a principle of representation learning that involves finding a compact representation of the data. The goal is to map the high-dimensional input data into a smaller, more efficient form.

concepts.name: Prediction
concepts.definition: Prediction is one of two general principles for learning good vector embeddings without a supervised task, requiring the system to be able to predict missing data when that data is held out.

concepts.name: K-means
concepts.definition: K-means is an algorithm that finds k different clusters within a dataset, where each cluster is represented by its mean. It maps data points to integers such that each point is as close as possible to the mean of its assigned cluster.

concepts.name: Vector quantized autoencoder
concepts.definition: Vector quantized autoencoder is a model that is functionally the same as k-means, but it uses a non-linear function for the encoding process. This model aims to encode data into a set of integers while minimizing reconstruction error.

concepts.name: Pretext task
concepts.definition: A pretext task is a fake label or task derived from the raw data itself, which allows the model to switch from unsupervised learning to the mathematical machinery of supervised learning. These tasks guide the model to learn useful representations from the data.

concepts.name: Imputation
concepts.definition: Imputation is a process where a portion of the input data, such as a matrix or tensor, is masked. The data is then passed through an encoder and decoded to predict the missing, masked part of the original input.

concepts.name: Masked autoencoder
concepts.definition: A masked autoencoder is a model where random chunks of the input data are masked. The model is then trained to predict these missing chunks, which is conceptually similar to an autoencoder.

concepts.name: Similarity-based representation learning
concepts.definition: Similarity-based representation learning is a concept within representation learning that explores what makes a good representation, often by building a metric space. This approach includes introducing metric learning and contrastive representation learning to self-supervise the idea of building that metric space.

concepts.name: Metric learning
concepts.definition: Linear metric learning involves learning a linear transformation $z = Wx$. This approach contrasts with deep metric learning, which seeks a nonlinear transformation $z = f(x)$ where $f(x)$ is implemented by a neural network.

concepts.name: Contrastive representation learning
concepts.definition: Contrastive representation learning is a method that combines ideas from metric learning and self-supervision to build representation spaces without requiring explicit supervision.

concepts.name: Geometric similarity
concepts.definition: Geometric similarity describes the structural consistency of data, where physical or structural features remain similar regardless of changes in external factors like lighting, pose, or orientation. This concept is applied to build representations that enable finding items similar to a given query.

concepts.name: Representation
concepts.definition: Representation is the learned feature space where data points are mapped and organized by the model. The representation space determines how closely related items, such as two different images of a golden retriever, will cluster together.

concepts.name: Compact
concepts.definition: Compact means that a representation is not too large. A compact representation avoids having more capacity than is actually needed.

concepts.name: Explanatory
concepts.definition: Explanatory means that the representation is sufficient to capture the dimensions that matter in the original data. Unlike compactness, which focuses on minimizing the amount of information, explanatory ensures that the retained information is relevant and meaningful.

concepts.name: Linear separability
concepts.definition: Linear separability is a state where categorization is very easy. This is because one can simply draw lines between different objects in the space.

concepts.name: Complexity measure
concepts.definition: Complexity measure is a tool designed to predict a model's generalization ability by analyzing the structure of its learned representation. These measures specifically examine the representation's geometry, focusing on the consistency and separation of similar and dissimilar data points, as well as its robustness to small perturbations.

concepts.name: Geometry of the representation
concepts.definition: Geometry of the representation refers to structural properties of the learned representation, specifically examining consistency and separation. Consistency measures how tightly together things that are the same are grouped, while separation measures how far apart things that are different are placed.

concepts.name: Robustness to perturbation
concepts.definition: Robustness to irrelevant perturbations ensures that when an input is changed in a way that is considered irrelevant, the resulting feature representation does not change or move significantly within the embedding space.

concepts.name: Class boundary
concepts.definition: Class boundary is the limit in the latent space where moving further causes the generated image to cross into a different category. Understanding this boundary is crucial for defining the reasonable limits of a specific class.

concepts.name: Good representation
concepts.definition: A good representation is a feature set that is compact and explanatory, ensuring that data belonging to the same classes are close together while different classes are well separated.

concepts.name: Contrastive learning
concepts.definition: Contrastive learning is a method where a model is trained by providing information about the similarity or dissimilarity between pairs of inputs, which helps the model understand both similarity and small contrasting differences.

concepts.name: Mahalanobis distance
concepts.definition: Mahalanobis distance is a distance measure between two points that is explicitly defined by a positive semidefinite matrix $A$. Learning an optimal $A$ results in a transformation that maximally preserves similarity and difference.

concepts.name: Representation space
concepts.definition: Representation space is the embedding environment learned by a model, which can possess characteristics like uniformity depending on the learning objective. Contrastive learning, for example, tends to learn a uniform representation space, whereas supervised learning does not necessarily produce one.

concepts.name: Deep metric learning
concepts.definition: Deep metric learning is the process of trying to learn a nonlinear transformation $z = f(x)$, where $f(x)$ is a neural network. This approach maps data into a space that preserves similarity between desired positive pairs and dissimilarity between negative pairs.

concepts.name: Normalizing representation
concepts.definition: Normalizing representation is the technique of enforcing that all distances live on the hypersphere. This allows similarity to be measured by the angle between representations, making inner products a viable alternative to Euclidean distance.

concepts.name: Nonlinear transformation
concepts.definition: Nonlinear transformation is a mapping $z = f(x)$, where $f(x)$ is a neural network, which differs from a simple linear projection $z = Wx$. This allows the model to learn complex representations that keep similar data points close and dissimilar data points far apart.

concepts.name: Hypersphere
concepts.definition: A hypersphere is a geometric space onto which data is normalized, enforcing that all representations lie on its surface.

concepts.name: Contrastive loss
concepts.definition: Contrastive loss is a loss function that explicitly encourages the learned representation to exhibit both alignment and uniformity. This encourages concentration and separation within the representation space.

concepts.name: Triplet loss
concepts.definition: Triplet loss is a loss function that operates on three different embeddings—an anchor, a positive, and a negative example—which are derived from three input images run through the same convolutional neural network. This loss is then used to back propagate through the graph, training the network to improve the representation.

concepts.name: Negative example
concepts.definition: Negative examples are data points used during training that are distinct from the current point, and having a large number of these examples significantly improves performance.

concepts.name: Anchor example
concepts.definition: Anchor example is the reference image used in the triplet loss calculation. It serves as the central point against which the similarity of the positive and negative examples is measured.

concepts.name: Hard negative
concepts.definition: Hard negative is a negative example that provides a necessary training signal because the model is failing to adequately separate it from the positive example. These examples are crucial for training because easy examples do not provide the signal needed to move the representations apart.

concepts.name: Nearest neighbors
concepts.definition: Nearest neighbors refers to the data points in the entire dataset that are closest to a given image when queried within the representation space. Finding these neighbors is a difficult problem, even when supervision is used.

concepts.name: Hard negative mining
concepts.definition: Hard negative mining is a technique used to accelerate learning by actively searching for difficult negative examples. This process helps the model improve quickly by focusing on challenging data points.

concepts.name: Misplaced negative
concepts.definition: Misplaced negative is a hard negative example that the model has incorrectly placed closer to the anchor than a positive example. Finding these examples helps accelerate the learning process.

concepts.name: Confounding dimension
concepts.definition: Confounding dimension is a feature, such as pose or background color, that makes images appear similar based on many dimensions but is not relevant to the desired semantic categorization. Confounding dimensions are features that the model needs to be invariant to in order to recognize what should truly be similar.

concepts.name: Invariant
concepts.definition: Invariant refers to a desired property where the model is trained to ignore specific variations, such as pose or background color, when determining similarity. This allows the model to focus on the core semantic meaning of the image.

concepts.name: Self-supervised contrastive representation learning
concepts.definition: Self-supervised contrastive representation learning is a specific type of contrastive representation learning that uses self-supervision to build representation spaces without explicit labels.

concepts.name: Encoder
concepts.definition: An encoder is a function that maps input data onto a hypersphere, serving as the core component in the self-supervised representation learning setup.

concepts.name: Crossentropy loss
concepts.definition: Crossentropy loss is a function used to discriminate classes based on similarity, aiming to explicitly pull positive pairs together and push negative pairs apart.

concepts.name: Positive pair
concepts.definition: A positive pair consists of two data examples that belong to the same class or are considered similar. The model is trained to ensure these pairs are close together in the learned feature space.

concepts.name: Augmentation
concepts.definition: Augmentation is a process where an input data point is perturbed in various ways. This perturbation forces the model to learn invariance to those changes.

concepts.name: Supervision
concepts.definition: Supervision refers to having explicit definitions of similarity or dissimilarity based on categories. Self-supervision, conversely, forces the model to learn that an input data point is similar to itself after being subjected to various augmentations, without relying on predefined categories.

concepts.name: Linear classifier
concepts.definition: Linear classifier is a model that uses a simple slice through the hypersphere representation to separate data. This classifier is guaranteed to be linearly separable provided that similar examples are mapped close together and different examples are mapped far apart on the hypersphere.

concepts.name: Self-supervised signal
concepts.definition: Self-supervised signal is a method of supervising models without requiring expensive, handcrafted human-generated labels. This signal is derived from the data itself, allowing the model to learn representations automatically.

concepts.name: Positive and negative pairs
concepts.definition: Positive and negative pairs are sets of data samples used to train the model. Positive pairs are examples that should be considered similar, while negative pairs are examples that should be considered dissimilar.

concepts.name: Mutual information
concepts.definition: Mutual information is a mathematical concept used to motivate contrastive loss by maximizing a lower bound on the information shared between views of the same thing; however, maximizing it alone can worsen downstream performance.

concepts.name: Concentration alignment
concepts.definition: Concentration alignment is a property where data samples belonging to the same class are positioned close together within the representation space. This ensures that similar inputs are mapped to similar locations.

concepts.name: Separation
concepts.definition: Separation is the property that data samples belonging to different classes are positioned far apart in the feature space. This ensures that distinct categories are clearly distinguishable from one another.

concepts.name: Uniformity
concepts.definition: Uniformity describes the desired state where dissimilar samples are pushed apart equally, often aiming to cover the entire hypersphere. This ensures that the feature space is utilized evenly across all data points.

concepts.name: Unsupervised contrastive learning
concepts.definition: Unsupervised contrastive learning is a method that enforces uniformity across data points by pulling similar samples together while pushing dissimilar samples apart. This process is used to structure the feature space without relying on explicit class labels.

concepts.name: Alignment
concepts.definition: Alignment is a metric used to quantify how well features are aligned in a representation. This is achieved by looking at the expectation over the distance between features for positive pairs.

concepts.name: Gaussian potential
concepts.definition: Gaussian potential is a transformation used to quantify uniformity, allowing researchers to look at the logarithm of the expected pairwise Gaussian potential. This potential is essentially defined as e to the minus squared distance between features.

concepts.name: Uniform distribution on the hypersphere
concepts.definition: Uniform distribution on the hypersphere is the unique measure that minimizes the expected pairwise potential between negative pairs. This distribution is the solution that maximally spreads out points on the hypersphere.

concepts.name: Explicit contrastive loss
concepts.definition: Explicit contrastive loss connects the concepts of alignment and uniformity, and its mathematical properties are understood by analyzing its asymptotic behavior. Specifically, the loss can be reformulated by taking the limit as the number of negative samples goes to infinity, resulting in a combination of two expectation terms.

concepts.name: Projection head
concepts.definition: A projection head is a simple learned component, such as a linear projection or a small multilayer perceptron, that maps the feature representation into a separate space. This projection allows the contrastive loss to be calculated in a space that helps improve downstream performance.

concepts.name: Linear probe
concepts.definition: Linear probe is a technique where a representation space is used, and a simple linear projection is learned with supervision to act as the categorizer. This projection is trained to map the learned representation into the final classification output.

concepts.name: Similarity measure
concepts.definition: Similarity measure is a metric used in contrastive learning to determine which data points are considered similar (positive pairs) and which are considered different (negative pairs) relative to the problem of interest.

concepts.name: Contrastive objective
concepts.definition: Contrastive objective is a learning method that aims to structure data representations by making similar inputs close together in the embedding space while ensuring dissimilar inputs are far apart.

concepts.name: Open set clustering problem
concepts.definition: Open set clustering problem is the challenge of grouping data points into clusters even when the model encounters categories or data points it has never seen during training. Contrastive objectives are explicitly better at solving this problem than standard classification methods.

concepts.name: Semiorthogonal matrix
concepts.definition: Semiorthogonal matrix is a rectangular matrix that is not fully orthogonal. This type of matrix is derived from operations like setting singular values to one.

concepts.name: Representation
concepts.definition: Representation is a good mapping of data points that deep learning aims to learn, allowing semantically different data points to be separated from each other within the network's output.

concepts.name: Linearly separable
concepts.definition: Linearly separable refers to a representation where data points from different classes are separated from each other, ideally using a linear boundary at the end of the network.

concepts.name: Neural network architecture
concepts.definition: Neural network architecture is the specific structure of a neural network, which the lecture argues already expresses an opinion about the similarity of data points even before the network is trained.

concepts.name: Interpolation
concepts.definition: Interpolation is an operator that allows for the combination of two complete data systems—including the data set, latent space, generator, and inverse—to generate a new object. This process extends standard interpolation by operating over the entire data plus generator system.

concepts.name: Linear interpolation
concepts.definition: Linear interpolation is a method of smoothly transitioning between two points in a space by moving along a straight line. When performed across certain boundaries, it can result in unnatural or jarring shifts in the generated data.

concepts.name: Function class
concepts.definition: Function class is the set of possible mathematical functions that a machine learning model can use to represent the relationship in the data. Choosing a function class dictates the complexity and type of patterns the model can learn.

concepts.name: Kernel methods
concepts.definition: Kernel methods are a type of function space approach that uses bump functions, which are arranged to fit the data. These methods are related to Gaussian processes.

concepts.name: Bump function
concepts.definition: A bump function is a function, such as a Gaussian or a curvy shape, that is placed at the location of each input data point. These functions are used as the building blocks to construct a function that can fit the data.

concepts.name: Reproducing kernel Hilbert space
concepts.definition: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space is a specific function space, denoted as big F, that is formed when the number of bump functions is allowed to go to infinity. This space contains all functions that can be decomposed in the specific form described by the kernel methods.

concepts.name: Stochastic process
concepts.definition: A stochastic process is a method used to sample random functions, which serves as a classic alternative way of constructing function spaces for machine learning.

concepts.name: Posterior distribution of functions
concepts.definition: The posterior distribution of functions is the distribution of functions that results from conditioning the initial distribution on the specific training data.

concepts.name: Kernel interpolator
concepts.definition: A kernel interpolator is a single, smooth function that is equivalent to the mean of the distribution of functions consistent with the data.

concepts.name: Gaussian process
concepts.definition: Gaussian process is a type of random function used in this context, where the function values sampled at different points are related by a specific covariance structure.

concepts.name: Infinitely wide
concepts.definition: Infinitely wide refers to a condition where the width of all hidden layers in a neural network is made infinite. Under this condition, the distribution of randomly sampled functions is equivalent to a Gaussian process.

concepts.name: Covariance structure
concepts.definition: Covariance structure is the component of a Gaussian process that dictates the shape of the standard deviations and the overall appearance of the resulting function. Machine learning practitioners select this structure when applying Gaussian processes.

concepts.name: Mean function
concepts.definition: Mean function is the expected value of the random functions generated by the Gaussian process, which is reasonable to be much smoother than the individual random functions. This function provides the predicted value at a given point.

concepts.name: Standard deviation
concepts.definition: Standard deviation is a measure of the variability around the mean function, which is expected to shrink to zero directly on the observed data points. This measure is also expected to grow as one moves away from the data.

concepts.name: Random vector
concepts.definition: Random vector is a vector whose entries are random variables. It is used in this context to represent a set of random values that can be plotted on an axis.

concepts.name: Multivariate normal random vector
concepts.definition: Multivariate Gaussian is the specific type of joint distribution that results from the definition of a Gaussian process. This distribution applies to any collection of inputs, including both known and unknown points.

concepts.name: Gaussian vector
concepts.definition: Gaussian vector is a random vector where the simplest form has independent and identically distributed (iid) coordinates, while a general form is defined using a covariance matrix.

concepts.name: Covariance function
concepts.definition: Covariance function is the element that describes the covariance between a function at two different inputs, serving as the generalization of the covariance matrix.

concepts.name: Conditioning with Gaussian vectors
concepts.definition: Conditioning with Gaussian vectors is the specific mathematical process used to find the conditional distribution when dealing with Gaussian vectors. This process yields a closed-form expression for the mean and standard deviation of the predicted point.

concepts.name: Neural Network Gaussian Process Correspondence
concepts.definition: Neural Network Gaussian Process Correspondence is a result stating that if a neural network is sufficiently wide and its weights are randomly sampled, the distribution of outputs for any finite collection of inputs is a multivariate Gaussian.

concepts.name: Distribution of functions
concepts.definition: Distribution of functions is a probabilistic, Gaussian distribution of possible functions that the model generates when considering the data. This distribution includes a mean function, but also contains a small probability of generating highly bizarre or horrible functions that deviate significantly from the mean.

concepts.name: Overparameterized neural network
concepts.definition: Overparameterized neural network refers to a network that is very wide, yet retains the ability to represent simple functions. This characteristic means that the network's width does not automatically imply overfitting.

concepts.name: Central limit theorem
concepts.definition: Central limit theorem is a mathematical principle that allows things to converge to a Gaussian distribution when applied over the width of a network. This theorem is the basis for the construction that requires the network to be infinitely wide.

concepts.name: Kernel function
concepts.definition: Kernel function is the covariance function chosen to define the Gaussian process. The design and choice of this function determine the characteristics of the model.

concepts.name: Squared exponential kernel
concepts.definition: Squared exponential kernel is a typical kernel function introduced in Gaussian processes. It is defined by a specific functional form, such as e to the negative x minus x-prime squared.

concepts.name: Multivariate central limit theorem
concepts.definition: Multivariate central limit theorem is the main mathematical tool used to prove the correspondence between infinitely wide neural networks and Gaussian processes. This theorem generalizes the standard central limit theorem to Gaussian vectors.

concepts.name: Weight initialization
concepts.definition: Weight initialization is the process of setting initial values for the weights in a neural network. For specific theoretical results to hold, the initialization must use a variance of 1 over fan-in.

concepts.name: Compositional arccosine kernel
concepts.definition: Compositional arccosine kernel is a particular mathematical function that corresponds to the network architecture. This kernel is derived from the expectation of the network output, specifically the product of the network output evaluated at two different inputs.

concepts.name: Xavier initialization
concepts.definition: Xavier initialization is an initialization method that uses 1 over fan-in, which is the standard built into PyTorch. This method is used because it is good at preserving activation magnitudes at initialization.

concepts.name: Diffusion model
concepts.definition: A diffusion model starts with a structured, complicated object and adds noise globally to every data point until it reaches a very simple distribution that can be sampled from. The model is then supervised to reverse this process, which is used for generation.

concepts.name: Density function
concepts.definition: A density function assigns a normalized score to the data. This function is used to represent the data generating process.

concepts.name: Energy functions
concepts.definition: An energy function gives an unnormalized score to the data. This function is parameterized by weights and biases, mapping data to a numerical value.

concepts.name: Generative AI
concepts.definition: Generative AI is the area of generative modeling where the goal is to have algorithms that make things that look like data. This focus is on creating data rather than analyzing or classifying existing data.

concepts.name: Image-to-image model
concepts.definition: Image-to-image model is a type of model that generates an image output. This output is conditioned on an input image, allowing it to predict what an image would look like under different scanning conditions.

concepts.name: Distribution over objects Y
concepts.definition: Distribution over objects Y is the concept where a neural network maps from an input space X to a probability distribution across possible outputs Y. This means the model predicts a range of possibilities rather than just a single, definitive answer.

concepts.name: Space of probability distributions
concepts.definition: Space of probability distributions is the set, denoted by P, that contains all possible probability distributions over the output space Y. This concept allows the model to output a distribution of possibilities rather than a single object.

concepts.name: Categorical distribution
concepts.definition: Categorical distribution is a probability mass function used to represent the likelihood of a discrete outcome, such as predicting the next word or pixel. The model outputs a probability distribution over all possible classes or vocabulary items.

concepts.name: Random variable
concepts.definition: Random variable is a set of possible outcomes, or atoms, that is characterized by a specific distribution. Uppercase letters are used in this course to denote these variables.

concepts.name: Probability mass function
concepts.definition: Probability mass function is a mapping that assigns scalars between 0 and 1 to data points. The sum of all these probabilities over all possible outcomes must equal 1.

concepts.name: Probability density function
concepts.definition: Probability density function is used for continuous variables and describes the probability distribution over a continuous space. The total probability is found by integrating the density function, and the densities themselves are required to be nonnegative.

concepts.name: Realization
concepts.definition: Realization is a specific sample or outcome that a random variable takes on from its set of possible values. This specific outcome is indicated using a lowercase variable name.

concepts.name: Implicit distribution
concepts.definition: Implicit distribution is the interpretation that a neural network, even when predicting a single value like in regression, is actually representing a probability distribution over possible outcomes.

concepts.name: Generator
concepts.definition: Generator is a neural network that functions as a deterministic function but is conditioned on a random variable. This conditioning allows the generator to produce multiple randomized outputs from a single input command.

concepts.name: Latent variable
concepts.definition: Latent variable is any variable that determines the appearance of the data but is not directly observable. Latent variables underlie the causal process of generating the data.

concepts.name: Direct approach
concepts.definition: Direct approach is a method that learns a function capable of directly sampling random generated data points, starting from noise or latent variables. This function outputs the generated data directly.

concepts.name: Indirect approach
concepts.definition: Indirect approach is a classical characterization where the model learns a scoring function from existing data. This function assigns a high score to values where the observed data resides.

concepts.name: Likelihood of the data
concepts.definition: Likelihood of the data is a mapping that takes data and assigns it a scalar value. If this likelihood represents a density, the resulting scalar must be nonnegative.

concepts.name: Implicit generative model
concepts.definition: Implicit generative model refers to a sampling procedure that implies a probability distribution from which samples could be drawn. This distribution is implied by the sampler rather than being explicitly defined.

concepts.name: Sampling
concepts.definition: Sampling is the phase where the trained model is used to generate new data samples. This process is equivalent to the testing phase for a neural network fit to data.

concepts.name: Scoring function
concepts.definition: Scoring function is a function that places a high score where the data lives, which can be a probability distribution or an energy function. This function allows for the subsequent sampling of new data from the learned distribution.

concepts.name: Training
concepts.definition: Training is the initial phase where the model is taught by being given a large number of examples. During this phase, the model learns the parameters of its function.

concepts.name: Markov chain Monte Carlo
concepts.definition: Markov chain Monte Carlo is a sampling method that only requires relative probabilities to function. This allows the sampler to draw points from the implied distribution even without a normalized density.

concepts.name: Density model
concepts.definition: A density model is a mapping that assigns a likelihood to every point within a data space, and this mapping is parameterized by weights and biases.

concepts.name: Max likelihood objective
concepts.definition: The max likelihood objective is the machine learning goal of maximizing the probability that the model places on the training data, which are samples from an unknown data generating process.

concepts.name: KL divergence
concepts.definition: KL divergence is a measure used to quantify the difference between two probability distributions, specifically comparing the model's distribution to the true, unknown data generating distribution. Minimizing this divergence is the objective used to fit the model so that its distribution closely approximates the distribution from which the training data was sampled.

concepts.name: Expectation
concepts.definition: Expectation is the integral of the probability distribution multiplied by a function of the data. It represents the average value of a function under a given probability distribution.

concepts.name: Parameterization
concepts.definition: Parameterization is the method by which a distribution is defined by a finite set of values, such as a network output. The vector output by a network must contain all the necessary parameters of the distribution family being considered.

concepts.name: Energy-based model
concepts.definition: Energy-based models are a type of generative model that uses an energy function instead of a probability density function. This energy function represents an unnormalized probability score for the data.

concepts.name: Boltzmann distribution
concepts.definition: Boltzmann distribution is a probability function derived from an energy function. This distribution is calculated as the exponential of the negative energy divided by a normalization constant.

concepts.name: Energy ratio
concepts.definition: Energy ratio is the comparison of two exponential energy functions, where the ratio of $e^{-E_1}$ to $e^{-E_2}$ is equivalent to the ratio of the corresponding probabilities. Energy ratio allows for relative judgments of likelihood without requiring knowledge of the normalization constant, which is often intractable for probability densities.

concepts.name: Contrastive divergence
concepts.definition: Contrastive divergence is an algorithm that maximizes the likelihood of the density implied by the energy for an energy-based model. It works by balancing the energy placed on the data versus the energy placed by the model.

concepts.name: Normalization
concepts.definition: Normalization, also called the partition function, is the constant required to ensure the probability distribution is properly scaled. The gradient of this function is a critical component in the derivation of contrastive divergence.

concepts.name: Max likelihood density modeling
concepts.definition: Max likelihood density modeling is an objective where the goal is to maximize the probability density that the model assigns to the actual ground-truth data. This maximization process is how the model is trained to accurately represent the data distribution.

concepts.name: Supervised learning
concepts.definition: Supervised learning is a training method used to reverse the diffusion process by learning a mapping from random noise to images. This process is supervised by providing the model with the exact path to take, using pairs of noisy and less noisy data.

concepts.name: Diffusion process
concepts.definition: Diffusion process is a physical phenomenon where particles spread out randomly, eventually becoming uniformly distributed in a space. In the context of models, it refers to diffusing data in a high-dimensional data space.

concepts.name: Gaussian diffusion model
concepts.definition: Gaussian diffusion model is a framework that defines a data generating process starting from a simple distribution, such as a unit Gaussian, and maps it to complex data.

concepts.name: Forward process
concepts.definition: Forward process is the simple deterministic process that adds Gaussian noise to an image, converting the original data into increasingly noisy versions.

concepts.name: Reverse process
concepts.definition: Reverse process is the learned process that attempts to invert the forward noiser by predicting the mean of a Gaussian distribution over the less noisy image.

concepts.name: Denoiser
concepts.definition: Denoiser is the neural network trained to predict the less noisy image from the more noisy image, allowing the model to invert the noise addition.

concepts.name: Unit Gaussian
concepts.definition: Unit Gaussian is the simple distribution from which the data generating process starts, and it is also the asymptotic distribution that the data converges to as noise is added infinitely.

concepts.name: Categorical density modeling problem
concepts.definition: Categorical density modeling problem is a simple modeling task where the goal is to determine the probability distribution over a finite set of discrete outcomes, such as predicting the color of a single pixel given previous data.

concepts.name: Generator network
concepts.definition: Generator network is a neural network that takes a latent variable and maps it through to produce an image. The generator's goal is to synthesize synthetic images that are indistinguishable from real data.

concepts.name: Min-max game
concepts.definition: Min-max game is a type of adversarial game where the generator tries to minimize a specific objective while the discriminator tries to maximize the exact same objective. This competitive dynamic drives the generator to improve its output quality.

concepts.name: Prior distribution
concepts.definition: The prior distribution is a simple structure distribution, typically representing noise, which is used as the starting point for the generative process. This distribution is mapped to the complicated data distribution.

concepts.name: Encoder
concepts.definition: The encoder is a mapping function, denoted as f, that takes data as input and transforms it into a representation in the latent space. This function is central to the representation learning direction.

concepts.name: Variational autoencoder
concepts.definition: Variational autoencoder is a type of autoencoder designed to ensure that the latent space forms a simple distribution that can be sampled from.

concepts.name: Gaussian
concepts.definition: A Gaussian is a density model fitted to data using a maximum likelihood objective, which attempts to increase the density applied to where the data resides. The parameters that characterize a Gaussian are its mean and its variance.

concepts.name: Decoder
concepts.definition: Decoder is the second half of the autoencoder, which functions as a mapping from a latent vector to the data space.

concepts.name: Latent space
concepts.definition: Latent space is the set of encodings of an autoencoder that the Variational Autoencoder aims to structure into a simple distribution.

concepts.name: Mixture of Gaussians
concepts.definition: Mixture of Gaussians is a classical statistical model that combines multiple Gaussian distributions. This model is used to represent complex data distributions by summing several simpler Gaussian components.

concepts.name: Infinite mixture of Gaussians
concepts.definition: The Infinite mixture of Gaussians is a density model used to represent the data distribution. The VAE approximates this continuous distribution using a finite set of samples.

concepts.name: Likelihood
concepts.definition: Likelihood is the measure of how well a model assigns probability to the observed data. Maximizing the likelihood means perturbing parameters to increase the probability assigned to the data.

concepts.name: Marginal likelihood
concepts.definition: Marginal likelihood is the probability of the data obtained by integrating over all unobserved latent variables. This concept is crucial for fitting a latent variable model to data.

concepts.name: Latent variable model
concepts.definition: Latent variable model is a statistical framework that represents observed data using underlying, unobserved latent variables. The model is fitted to data by maximizing the marginal likelihood, which requires integrating over all possible settings of those latent variables.

concepts.name: Intractable integral
concepts.definition: Intractable integral is an integral that is difficult to calculate because there is no closed form solution for it. This difficulty prevents direct computation of the likelihood.

concepts.name: Normal distribution
concepts.definition: Normal distribution is a probability distribution defined by a mean and a variance, and it has a closed-form analytical form for its density. This density function is expressed using an exponential function involving the difference between the variable and the mean, scaled by the variance.

concepts.name: Objective function
concepts.definition: Objective function is the mathematical function, denoted L, that the model attempts to maximize during training. This function represents the data log likelihood, which measures how well the model fits the observed data.

concepts.name: Log likelihood
concepts.definition: Log likelihood is the natural logarithm of the marginal likelihood, $p(x)$, and it is used as the primary metric to maximize the model's fit to the data.

concepts.name: Expectation
concepts.definition: Expectation is the average value of a random variable, which is calculated by integrating over a distribution. In this context, the expectation represents the true likelihood of the data point $x$.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo estimate
concepts.definition: Monte Carlo estimator is a method used in the approximation step to estimate integrals by drawing samples. The variance of this estimator is inversely proportional to the number of samples used, specifically $1/M$.

concepts.name: Exponential samples
concepts.definition: Exponential samples refers to the intuition that covering a D-dimensional space requires a number of samples that grows exponentially with the dimension, suggesting that the required sample size depends exponentially on the dimension for a quality fit.

concepts.name: Importance sampling
concepts.definition: Importance sampling is a technique that approximates an integral by sampling from a distribution $q(z)$ that places higher density on the points that contribute significantly to the integral. This targeted sampling approach is designed to require far fewer samples than naive random sampling from the original distribution $p(z)$, where most samples would yield negligible contributions.

concepts.name: Decoder function
concepts.definition: Decoder function is the probability model that defines the probability of the data X given the latent variable Z. This function is one of the two pieces used to construct the full generative model.

concepts.name: Evidence lower bound
concepts.definition: The Evidence lower bound (ELBO) is a lower bound to the likelihood of the data under the model. This bound is derived using Jensen's inequality.

concepts.name: Reconstruction error
concepts.definition: Reconstruction error is the first term of the ELBO, which measures how different the decoded point is from the original input observation $x$. This term essentially quantifies the likelihood of the data given the latent representation.

concepts.name: Fundamental tension
concepts.definition: The Fundamental tension is the conflict between two requirements: pushing the latent space towards zero to create a compact shape, and preserving enough information to reconstruct the input data.

concepts.name: Ambiguity
concepts.definition: Ambiguity occurs when two different data points map to the same point or to overlapping Gaussian components in the latent space. This prevents the model from knowing which input point generated a specific latent representation, thus hindering reconstruction.

concepts.name: Reconstruction
concepts.definition: Reconstruction is the process where the model attempts to reproduce the original input point from its compressed latent representation. This process requires the model to preserve sufficient information during compression.

concepts.name: Representation learner
concepts.definition: Representation learner is a model component, such as an encoder, that is assessed for its independent utility beyond the primary task of generation. Representation learners are useful when the latent space they produce allows for meaningful, controllable variations in the output data.

concepts.name: Disentangled space
concepts.definition: Disentangled space is a representation where the data is mapped such that different dimensions correspond to independent factors of the input. This allows specific directions in the space to control specific properties of the generated data.

concepts.name: Activation space
concepts.definition: Activation space is the set of values produced by a network's internal layers as it processes data. Directions within this space can be examined to find structured representations of the input data.

concepts.name: Structured representation
concepts.definition: Structured representation is a learned feature set that allows a model to fit to the world effectively. This representation must capture factors that can parsimoniously explain the data.

concepts.name: Structured prediction
concepts.definition: Structured prediction is a data prediction problem where the output is a high-dimensional object that does not factorize into independent marginals. This setting is used when the dimensions of the predicted object have joint dependencies.

concepts.name: Unstructured prediction
concepts.definition: Unstructured prediction is a method where the system treats every pixel independently and outputs a continuous real number for those pixels. This approach implicitly assumes that the output dimensions factorize independently.

concepts.name: High-dimensional structured object
concepts.definition: High-dimensional structured object is the type of output that is not a single number or a single decision, but rather a complex object with internal structure. This object is the target of prediction in problems like speech recognition or protein structure prediction.

concepts.name: Independent random variables
concepts.definition: Independent random variables are variables whose probabilities factorize as a product. This concept is used in unstructured prediction to assume that all dimensions of the data are statistically separate.

concepts.name: Least squares regression
concepts.definition: Least squares regression is a classical point prediction method that minimizes the least squared objective over a training distribution. This method yields the mean or expected value of the data distribution, which can be a poor estimate because that mean may have zero density under the true data distribution.

concepts.name: Multimodal distribution
concepts.definition: Multimodal distribution is a data distribution that possesses more than one bump or mode. This type of distribution cannot be accurately modeled by a unimodal distribution, such as a Gaussian.

concepts.name: Objective function
concepts.definition: Objective function is the mathematical function that the learning algorithm seeks to optimize. The choice of this function dictates how the model is trained and what it learns.

concepts.name: Adversarial game
concepts.definition: Adversarial game is a process where the generator and discriminator play against each other to find an equilibrium. At this equilibrium, the generator outputs images that are indistinguishable to the discriminator from real images.

concepts.name: Conditional GAN
concepts.definition: Conditional GAN is a modification where the discriminator must look at both the input and the output to determine if the output is a realistic pair that matches the input data. This allows the discriminator to penalize if the output does not conform to the input relationship.

concepts.name: Patch discriminator
concepts.definition: Patch discriminator is an architecture where the discriminator examines every small patch of an image individually, rather than evaluating the entire photo at once. This allows the discriminator to make a prediction for each patch regarding whether it looks real or fake.

concepts.name: Second-order statistic of the data
concepts.definition: Second-order statistic of the data is a measure that requires two measurements to be observed, such as determining if an image is sharp or blurry. This statistic captures the difference between two pixels to assess the quality of the output.

concepts.name: Unstructured objective
concepts.definition: Unstructured objective is an objective function that only incentivizes the model to model the factorized distribution of the output. If used alone, this objective function provides no incentive for the model to capture joint dependencies between different dimensions of the output.

concepts.name: High-capacity hypothesis space
concepts.definition: High-capacity hypothesis space is the characteristic of deep learning models that allows them to contain many complex functions. This capacity enables deep learning to find complicated nonlinear functions that older, low-capacity algorithms could not.

concepts.name: Hallucination
concepts.definition: Hallucination is a guess generated by a generative model, where the output is a sample from the true distribution but is not necessarily accurate in its specific location or detail.

concepts.name: Mode collapse
concepts.definition: Mode collapse is a failure of a generator function where it outputs one or a few modes of the distribution that look realistic. Mode collapse prevents the model from capturing the full posterior, instead focusing only on a limited subset of the possible data variations.

concepts.name: Conditional prediction
concepts.definition: Conditional prediction is the process of taking text as input and predicting some other text as output. This method allows the model to generate a specific output based on a given input.

concepts.name: Conditional generative model
concepts.definition: A conditional generative model is a type of model designed to generate data, such as an image or text, based on specific input data. This process allows the model to learn from paired data, where the input and desired output are linked.

concepts.name: Prompting language models
concepts.definition: Prompting language models is the technique of giving a language model whatever input is desired to guide its output. This is the method used when interacting with large language models.

concepts.name: Transformer
concepts.definition: Transformer is a mechanism that allows different data types to be treated equally by converting everything into tokens for token-to-token mappings. This allows the system to process diverse data formats uniformly.

concepts.name: Image captioning
concepts.definition: Image captioning is the problem of taking an image and training a system to generate a descriptive caption. This caption is similar to text that might be written underneath an image online or used as alt text.

concepts.name: Language model
concepts.definition: Language model is a function that encodes textual input into a sequence of tokens. This encoding allows the model to translate the input text into a format that can condition the subsequent generative process.

concepts.name: Conditional model
concepts.definition: A conditional model is a type of generative model that takes specific input data to condition its output. This allows the model to perform general conditional prediction problems, such as generating an image based on a text prompt.

concepts.name: Unpaired translation
concepts.definition: Unpaired translation is the process of performing conditional modeling between two domains when there are no examples of the data from one domain paired with the data from the other. This technique allows for translation between modalities, such as converting a cartoon into a more realistic image.

concepts.name: Unpaired learning
concepts.definition: Unpaired learning is the problem of performing conditional modeling when only two sets of data, X and Y, are available, but no examples exist that show X paired with Y. This situation is often more common than having perfectly paired data.

concepts.name: Cycle consistency
concepts.definition: Cycle consistency is a constraint that requires the mapping from domain X to domain Y to be consistent with a backward mapping from Y back to X. This means that if data is transformed from X to Y and then back to X, it should arrive at its original starting point.

concepts.name: Human verifier in the loop
concepts.definition: Human verifier in the loop describes a deployment strategy where a human is actively involved in making corrections when an AI model's output is not right. This verification loop ensures that human intelligence is always present.

concepts.name: Decision support tools
concepts.definition: Decision support tools are machine learning systems that provide advice or highlight information, such as potential diagnoses. The human user is ultimately liable to verify the tool's output and make the final decision.

concepts.name: Independently and Identically Distributed
concepts.definition: Independently and Identically Distributed (IID) is a theoretical assumption in machine learning where the data used for training a model is drawn from the same distribution as the data used for inference. This ideal setting requires that the training distribution equals the test distribution, a condition the instructor notes is rarely true in the real world.

concepts.name: Distributional change
concepts.definition: Distributional change is a fundamental difference that occurs between the distribution of data used for training a model and the distribution of data encountered during deployment. This shift means the real-world data differs from the data the model was originally trained on.

concepts.name: Data poisoning
concepts.definition: Data poisoning is a failure mode where the evaluation of machine learning systems is constructed in a way that is artificially Independently and Identically Distributed (IID). This artificial construction fails to represent the true complexity or reality of the deployment environment.

concepts.name: Adversarial example
concepts.definition: Adversarial examples are types of perturbations that can cause a model to misclassify an input. These examples can often transfer across models if they were trained on the same data set.

concepts.name: Perturbation
concepts.definition: Perturbation is a small change applied to a given input image, which is designed to change the model's prediction without being noticeable to a human observer. This change is the variable that is optimized to maximize the model's misclassification.

concepts.name: Projected gradient ascent
concepts.definition: Projected gradient ascent is a technique used to update the data perturbation over time by taking a step in the direction of the gradient and then projecting the result back into a feasible set. This process ensures the perturbation obeys the optimization constraint that the change cannot be too big

concepts.name: Training adversarially
concepts.definition: Adversarial training is a method used during model training to make the model robust to non-robust features and adversarial perturbations. This training aims to achieve invariance to these non-robust features.

concepts.name: Nested optimization
concepts.definition: Nested optimization is a training framework involving two loops: an inner loop that finds the worst-case perturbation for a given image, and an outer loop that adjusts the model parameters to minimize the loss under that worst-case scenario.

concepts.name: Adversarial robustness
concepts.definition: Adversarial robustness is the property of a model that allows it to remain stable when faced with adversarial perturbations. This concept relates to the model's ability to maintain correct predictions even when the input data is slightly altered.

concepts.name: Out-of-Distribution
concepts.definition: Out-of-Distribution refers to data that falls outside the distribution of the data the model was trained on. This concept is contrasted with independently identically distributed data.

concepts.name: Shortcut
