concepts.definition: Shortcut is a feature that is correlated with the label in the training data but is not correlated with the label under realistic distribution shifts. Models will use these shortcuts and fail to generalize if those features are no longer correlated.

concepts.name: Subpopulation shift
concepts.definition: Subpopulation shift occurs when any given location or camera has its own unique distribution over the categories of interest. This means the local set of species or features interacting with a specific point differs from the overall training set.

concepts.name: Distributionally robust optimization
concepts.definition: Distributionally robust optimization is a method that assumes the worst-case data distribution shift might occur. It seeks to find a model that minimizes the loss in expectation over all possible distribution shifts on the dataset.

concepts.name: Class imbalance challenges
concepts.definition: Class imbalance challenges occur when a dataset has a disproportionate number of examples in one category. This can cause a model to ignore minority groups and still achieve a decent overall loss.

concepts.name: Domain adaptation
concepts.definition: Domain adaptation is a category of models that learns to align representations between a source domain and a target domain. This allows the model to generalize or adapt to a new target domain even if there is limited labeled data.

concepts.name: Failure mode
concepts.definition: Failure mode refers to the specific ways a model performs poorly, which can be diagnosed to reveal underlying biases present in the initial training data.

concepts.name: In-distribution training data
concepts.definition: In-distribution training data is the type of data that is representative of the domain where the model is expected to operate successfully.

concepts.name: Knowledge distillation
concepts.definition: Knowledge distillation is a technique where a smaller student model is trained to match the output distribution of a larger, fixed pretrained teacher model. This process allows the student model to learn the knowledge captured in the teacher's predictions.

concepts.name: Foundation models
concepts.definition: Foundation models are very large models that possess high general utility. These models require massive amounts of compute and resources to train.

concepts.name: In-context learning
concepts.definition: In-context learning is an inner loop process where the model is given several examples of the desired task before being asked to continue performing it. This allows the model to learn a task without requiring traditional gradient descent updates.

concepts.name: Few-shot learning
concepts.definition: Few-shot learning is the idea that one can learn to generalize from limited examples, recognizing similarity and patterns in a useful way even when very little data is available.

concepts.name: Prior knowledge
concepts.definition: Prior knowledge is the existing information and experience that humans use when learning something new. This knowledge is built from our experience in the world.

concepts.name: Mental model
concepts.definition: Mental model is a model that captures how the world operates, which people build through their experience. Different people can possess different mental models of the world.

concepts.name: Representation
concepts.definition: Representation is a model or a capture of how the world operates, embodying the prior knowledge built through experience. Representations are the useful structures that allow systems to learn new things efficiently, forming the basis for concepts and measures of similarity.

concepts.name: Transferring knowledge
concepts.definition: Transferring knowledge is the process of taking knowledge learned from a model trained on one task and applying it to a different, related task. This involves moving the learned structure from the initial model to a new application.

concepts.name: Pretaining
concepts.definition: Pretaining is the process of training a network's set of weights and biases on an initial task. Pretaining results in parameters (W and b) that can then be used to initialize a second network, allowing knowledge about the mapping to be transferred to a new application.

concepts.name: Downstream task
concepts.definition: A downstream task is a specific application for which a generally useful model can be made effective. These tasks represent the different problems the model is intended to solve after its initial training.

concepts.name: Glue
concepts.definition: Glue is a simple mechanism added into the model structure to transfer data and ensure it is in the correct format for the downstream task. This mechanism is used when the downstream task does not share the same structure as the original pretraining task.

concepts.name: Reprojection
concepts.definition: Reprojection is a mechanism applied when the input dimension remains constant but the output dimension needs to be increased. Reprojection involves taking the final output layer of the initial model and learning a new mapping to project the existing representation into the desired number of dimensions.

concepts.name: Modular building block
concepts.definition: Modular building block is a component of a deep learning model that can be taken from one system and inserted into another. This structure allows developers to reuse well-trained components and adapt them to new problems.

concepts.name: Catastrophic forgetting problem
concepts.definition: Catastrophic forgetting problem occurs when the model's weights change too significantly during training on new data, causing the model to lose the useful knowledge it previously learned from the original data.

concepts.name: Freezing most of the network
concepts.definition: Freezing most of the network is a technique where the majority of the model's weights are kept constant, allowing only specific parts, such as the final layers, to be trained for the new task.

concepts.name: Small learning rates
concepts.definition: Small learning rates are a mechanism that prevents the model from moving too much in any direction during a training step.

concepts.name: Early stopping
concepts.definition: Early stopping is a method that utilizes a validation set to decide when to halt training, preventing the model from training excessively and forgetting its original knowledge.

concepts.name: Designing a benchmark
concepts.definition: Designing a benchmark for your data set involves understanding how to compare across different choices so you can try things and see how they are affecting the performance of your model. This process is crucial because custom problems often require testing to determine the best structure for a system.

concepts.name: Model compression
concepts.definition: Model compression is a set of mechanisms used to reduce the size of a large machine learning model while maintaining its accuracy. This process is distinct from distillation, which uses training to match characteristics, and includes techniques like pruning or quantization.

concepts.name: Unsupervised domain adaptation
concepts.definition: Unsupervised domain adaptation is a method where a model is trained to perform well on a set of data without having any training labels available in the target domain. The goal is to leverage labeled source data to improve performance on unlabeled target data.

concepts.name: Adversarial approach
concepts.definition: An adversarial approach involves training a model using both source and target data where the model is simultaneously trained to predict the desired category while being trained to fail at predicting the domain it came from. This mechanism forces the representations across the two domains to align.

concepts.name: Distillation
concepts.definition: Distillation is a mechanism to transfer knowledge by training a student model. The student model uses predictions from a source model on target data as weak supervision, aiming to learn something useful that is better than the raw predictions.

concepts.name: Soft target
concepts.definition: Soft target is a predictive distribution provided by a teacher model, offering more information than a simple ground truth class label. Soft targets convey input-specific similarity, indicating how an input relates to various categories—for example, showing a dog-like image is similar to a cat, but very different from a bear.

concepts.name: Teacher model
concepts.definition: Teacher model is a large, often pretrained model whose outputs are fixed and used to guide the training of a smaller student model. The teacher model provides the soft targets that the student attempts to replicate.

concepts.name: Student model
concepts.definition: Student model is a model being trained to distill knowledge from a fixed, pre-trained teacher model. The training objective requires the student model's predictions to closely match the distribution of predictions generated by the teacher model.

concepts.name: Contrastive learning
concepts.definition: Contrastive learning is a method used to supervise internal embeddings within a model by forcing them to be similar to a target representation. This process is used to ensure that the student model's representation matches the teacher's representation, rather than just matching the final output.

concepts.name: Ensemble
concepts.definition: Ensemble is a collection of multiple different models whose combined predictions are often more predictive than any single model. Distillation can be applied to this ensemble by training a single model to match the distribution of the outputs from all the constituent models.

concepts.name: Pruning
concepts.definition: Pruning is a method of model compression that involves explicitly removing weights from a model. This technique is highly computationally efficient because it simply deletes parts of the existing model structure.

concepts.name: Prompt engineering
concepts.definition: Prompt engineering is a new paradigm of research where a clever method is used to instruct a large language model to perform tasks for the user. This involves providing specific instructions or examples to guide the model's output, such as asking it to determine the sentiment of a review.

concepts.name: Soft prompting
concepts.definition: Soft prompting is a method that optimizes small continuous task-specific vectors while the language or the model parameters remain frozen. Soft prompting essentially attempts to find the optimal input words to use when interacting with the model.

concepts.name: Chain-of-thought prompting
concepts.definition: Chain-of-thought prompting is a technique that demonstrates an answer containing reasoning, which encourages the model to answer with logic. This method increases the likelihood that the model will provide a correct answer.

concepts.name: Meta-learning
concepts.definition: Meta-learning is the process of learning a model that is effective at transfer learning, allowing the model to adapt quickly to new tasks.

concepts.name: Distribution of inputs
concepts.definition: Distribution of inputs refers to the expected pattern of the data inputs. Knowing this distribution can be used to direct or accelerate learning or target a specific type of learning.

concepts.name: Manipulation
concepts.definition: Manipulation is an operator that allows for changing the data object, such as adding a bias term to the data. This gives a whole new kind of object for accessing and interacting with the data.

concepts.name: Composition
concepts.definition: Composition is the process of combining two data objects or generators in a way that is distinct from simple interpolation between them. This allows for combining and manipulating data objects in interesting ways.

concepts.name: Counterfactual reasoning
concepts.definition: Counterfactual reasoning is a method of understanding or testing hypotheses by generating possible alternative scenarios. This allows researchers to efficiently test how a model performs given different hypothetical data changes.

concepts.name: Disentangled factor of variation
concepts.definition: Disentangled dimension of variation refers to explicit latent space vectors that separate or factor out different underlying factors of variation within the data. These dimensions allow for the interpretation of specific changes, such as moving from winter to spring.

concepts.name: Manifold of natural images
concepts.definition: Natural image manifold is a nonlinear data space, X, that represents the set of real images. Linear interpolation within this image space moves off the manifold, resulting in unrealistic images that do not match the statistics of real natural images.

concepts.name: Dimensions of variation
concepts.definition: Dimensions of variation are specific features or attributes within the data that the model learns correspond to certain types of predictions. These dimensions can be used to probe how a model is making its predictions.

concepts.name: Vector of direction
concepts.definition: A vector of direction is a calculated vector that represents the path between two mapped points in the latent space. This vector corresponds to a specific type of counterfactual change in the original input data.

concepts.name: Intermediate representation
concepts.definition: Intermediate representation is a layer within a model that can itself function as a latent space. These representations are sometimes found to be better latent representations than the initial input vector (z representation).

concepts.name: StyleGAN
concepts.definition: StyleGAN is a generative model used in this context to efficiently label data. It is employed to generate a representation of specific pixel vectors that can then be used to train a predictive model for part labels.

concepts.name: Latent distribution
concepts.definition: Latent distribution is the space that the data distribution maps to, and which also maps back to the data distribution. This correspondence allows for mapping between the two spaces, such as matching a color on the natural image manifold to the same color in the latent space.

concepts.name: Data plus plus space
concepts.definition: Data plus plus space is a space derived from generative models where one can explore counterfactuals. This space allows researchers to understand why an image was classified in a certain way.

concepts.name: StyleSpace explanation approach
concepts.definition: StyleSpace explanation approach is a method that attempts to find the top K latent space directions of variation. These directions are chosen because they will most significantly affect which class a model predicts.

concepts.name: Underlying bias in training data
concepts.definition: Underlying bias in training data refers to dimensions of bias captured by the model. These dimensions reflect patterns present in the training data itself, such as the correlation between ear shape and species.

concepts.name: Dimensions of bias
concepts.definition: Dimensions of bias are specific variations that capture biases, which may be related to the fairness or equity of a deployed model. These dimensions can be analyzed to understand how they affect a model's predictions.

concepts.name: Explainability mechanism
concepts.definition: An explainability mechanism is a method used to understand how a model functions, allowing experts to verify if the model is using appropriate features. This process can build trust in a model by confirming its reasoning.

concepts.name: Latent space variation
concepts.definition: Latent space variation refers to the hidden, underlying variations within the data that must be discovered and manually analyzed. Finding these variations requires significant effort to understand the model's behavior.

concepts.name: Contrastive learning
concepts.definition: Contrastive learning is a mechanism for training models where the objective is to ensure that representations of similar data points are close together while representations of dissimilar data points are pushed far apart.

concepts.name: Diversity versus fidelity
concepts.definition: Diversity versus fidelity is a trade-off in training signal usefulness, balancing whether the training samples are highly different from each other (diversity) or nearly identical (fidelity).

concepts.name: Generation-augmented data
concepts.definition: Generation-augmented data is data that has been enhanced or supplemented using a generative model. This type of data allows for applying standard data operations, such as interpolation or manipulation, to potentially label data efficiently.

concepts.name: Model collapse
concepts.definition: Model collapse is a vicious cycle that occurs when a model is trained on more generated data than real data. This process can cause the model to lose parts of its original distribution that were present in the real data.

concepts.name: Manifold collapse
concepts.definition: Manifold collapse is a concern where, if a model is trained on more generated data than real data, it enters a vicious cycle. This process causes the model to lose parts of its original distribution that were captured in the real data due to the distribution of the generated data.

concepts.name: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning
concepts.definition: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) is a seminal work that attempts to learn an initial set of parameters such that the model can be easily adapted using only a few steps of stochastic gradient descent.

concepts.name: Scaling laws
concepts.definition: Scaling law is a principle that describes how a model's or algorithm's behavior changes as a function of increasing resources or input complexity. Scaling laws are used to predict how models will perform in the future.

concepts.name: Compute
concepts.definition: Compute is one of the three fundamental resources used in training models, calculated by multiplying the number of steps taken by the batch size.

concepts.name: Flops
concepts.definition: Flops (Floating Point Operations) is the unit used to measure compute, representing the number of floating point operations performed on the hardware.

concepts.name: Performance
concepts.definition: Performance is a measure of the model's quality, which is quantified in bits per word and relates to the cross-entropy of the next-word prediction.

concepts.name: Cross-entropy of the next-word prediction
concepts.definition: Cross-entropy of the next-word prediction is a metric related to the model's accuracy, where a lower value indicates that the model is making more accurate predictions.

concepts.name: Loss
concepts.definition: Loss is the metric used to measure the performance of the model, which is plotted against training factors to observe scaling behavior. The goal of training is to achieve a lower loss.

concepts.name: Downstream performance
concepts.definition: Downstream performance refers to the predictive capability of a model on specific tasks or benchmarks, such as passing math tests or coding problems, rather than just the training loss. Scaling laws can be applied to predict trends in this type of performance.

concepts.name: Data points
concepts.definition: Data points (D) refers to the number of individual examples used in the training dataset, which is a critical resource for scaling. This term specifically refers to the quantity of data, not dimensionality or depth.

concepts.name: Compute budget
concepts.definition: Compute budget (C) is the total computational effort, measured in flops, required to train a model of a specific size on a given dataset. This budget is used to determine the optimal number of parameters and data points.

concepts.name: Flops (Floating Point Operations)
concepts.definition: Flops is the unit of measurement used to quantify the total computational effort or compute budget required for training a model. It is the metric that the scaling laws paper focused on for analyzing resource allocation.

concepts.name: Data set size (D)
concepts.definition: Data set size is the independent variable plotted on the x-axis, representing the total number of tokens the model is trained on.

concepts.name: Model size
concepts.definition: Model size is one of the three fundamental resources, referring to the number of parameters in the model.

concepts.name: Power law relationship
concepts.definition: Power law relationship is a mathematical relationship observed in data where the points form a straight line when plotted on a log-log plot, indicating a specific scaling behavior.

concepts.name: Alpha
concepts.definition: Alpha is a constant parameter within the power law that determines the shape of the relationship. This constant depends on the specific properties of the data, the task, or the architecture being used.

concepts.name: Test loss
concepts.definition: Test loss is the variable that exhibits a power law relationship with resources, such as the number of parameters or the number of data points.

concepts.name: Log-log plot
concepts.definition: Log-log plot is a type of graph where both the x-axis and y-axis are plotted using logarithms, allowing a power law to appear as a straight line whose slope equals the power law's exponent.

concepts.name: High-dimensional statistics
concepts.definition: High-dimensional statistics is a field of study where the dependence on dimensionality influences the function fitting process, which can result in a specific scaling exponent.

concepts.name: Empirical
concepts.definition: Empirical describes observations that are derived from actual measurements of data, rather than being derived from theoretical first principles.

concepts.name: Pareto front
concepts.definition: Pareto front is the frontier that represents the optimal trade-offs among all different curves for various specific models and training configurations. This frontier is achieved when optimally using infinitely large data sets or selecting the perfect model size.

concepts.name: Frontier
concepts.definition: Frontier is the performance boundary that can be reached by sufficiently increasing the number of parameters in a model. This boundary itself follows a power law relationship when viewed in terms of the number of steps of gradient descent.

concepts.name: Extrapolate
concepts.definition: Extrapolate is the ability of a model to make valid predictions outside the range of data it was trained on. Extrapolation determines if a model's fitted relationship holds true across orders of magnitude.

concepts.name: Large language model
concepts.definition: Large language models are models that have been trained on massive datasets and possess a large number of parameters, a concept that predates modern deep learning. However, the instructor emphasizes that the success of contemporary models is due to the specific inductive bias provided by neural sequence models, not merely the quantity of data or parameters.

concepts.name: Next token prediction
concepts.definition: Next token prediction is the process where a language model assigns probability mass to the next word or token that should follow a given sequence of input text. This capability allows the model to generate coherent text based on the preceding input.

concepts.name: Count-based language model
concepts.definition: Count-based language model is an earlier generation of tool that estimates probabilities by getting big text corpora and counting word occurrences. These models were used to determine the plausibility of a particular decoding or sequence.

concepts.name: Perplexity
concepts.definition: Perplexity is a measure that quantifies the quality of a language model's predictions. It allows researchers to track the improvement in prediction ability when moving from classical count-based models to more advanced neural network architectures.

concepts.name: Sequence generation
concepts.definition: Sequence generation is the process where a language model is used to perform a task by generating a sequence of outputs, rather than merely ranking candidates. This shift allowed language models to be used directly for tasks like machine translation.

concepts.name: Next word prediction problem
concepts.definition: Next word prediction problem is a method where a language model is framed to guess the subsequent word in a sequence. This framing allows the model to be applied to tasks like translating a sentence from one language to another.

concepts.name: Next word prediction
concepts.definition: Next word prediction is a general purpose task where a model is trained to predict the subsequent word in a sequence of text. This task serves as a foundational system that can be leveraged for various downstream applications.

concepts.name: Masked language modeling
concepts.definition: Masked language modeling objective is a specific pretraining task where the model is trained to predict words that have been intentionally hidden or masked within a sentence. This objective allows the model to learn deep contextual relationships between words.

concepts.name: Pretrain and transfer mode
concepts.definition: Pretrain and transfer mode is an operational style where a model is first trained extensively on massive amounts of text data. Subsequently, the model is adapted to a specific downstream task using only a small amount of data.

concepts.name: Pretraining and prompting
concepts.definition: Pretraining and prompting is the current era of language model development where a highly general purpose next word prediction system is utilized. This allows for performing tasks without needing to modify the model's parameters or requiring downstream task data.

concepts.name: Hidden representation
concepts.definition: Hidden representation is the internal structure of a model where information is stored. This structure is where the parameter vector of a smaller model might be stored and updated across layers as more examples are ingested.

concepts.name: Large scale transfer effects
concepts.definition: Large scale transfer effects describe the ability of a model to apply general knowledge learned during massive pretraining to perform well on smaller, specific downstream tasks. This capability is what makes pretraining effective for various NLP applications.

concepts.name: Bidirectional transformer models
concepts.definition: Bidirectional transformer models are models trained using a masked language modeling paradigm that produces good representations of text. However, the way these models are set up prevents them from inherently generating the next word in a sequence.

concepts.name: Text generation
concepts.definition: Text generation is the process of creating textual output, such as in machine translation or summarization. This capability often requires a second stage that is trained specifically to generate the text.

concepts.name: Conditional text generation
concepts.definition: Conditional text generation is a type of text generation where the model is designed to output text based on specific input conditions. Models that perform this task are capable of predicting the next word in a sequence.

concepts.name: Downstream fine-tuning
concepts.definition: Downstream fine-tuning is a method where a pre-trained model is used as a starting point for subsequent tasks. This process typically involves adjusting the model to perform specific tasks after initial training.

concepts.name: Language model
concepts.definition: Language model is a system that predicts the probability of a word given a preceding sequence of words. To perform specific labeling tasks, such as sentiment classification, the model can be guided by providing examples within the input context.

concepts.name: Zero-shot prompting
concepts.definition: Zero-shot prompting is a method where the model is given a natural language description of the task without being provided explicit demonstrations. This allows the model to perform the task based solely on the instructions.

concepts.name: Few-shot prompting
concepts.definition: Few-shot prompting is a method that involves giving the model explicit demonstrations, such as pairs of input and output examples, for the task. This contrasts with zero-shot prompting, which relies only on instructions.

concepts.name: Synthetic data
concepts.definition: Synthetic data refers to a large collection of information, such as summaries, that is generated by the language model itself rather than being provided by a human.

concepts.name: Task-specific model
concepts.definition: A task-specific model is a model that is trained exclusively on targeted data sets for a single, particular task. This contrasts with modern approaches that use one large model for multiple tasks.

concepts.name: Novel step by step reasoning
concepts.definition: Novel step by step reasoning is the ability of a model to solve complicated problems that require sequential thought processes for individual problem instances. This capability goes beyond standard tasks that only require simple labeling or spitting out an answer.

concepts.name: Step by step thinking
concepts.definition: Step-by-step thinking is a technique where models are prompted to show their intermediate reasoning steps before providing a final answer. This method dramatically improves the quality of outputs for complex reasoning problems.

concepts.name: Few-shot paradigm
concepts.definition: Few-shot paradigm is an input method where the model is provided with a small number of examples to guide its reasoning or response. This approach is used because all necessary information is included within the input prompt.

concepts.name: Reasoning chain
concepts.definition: A reasoning chain is a sequence of intermediate steps that a model follows to solve a complex problem. Providing examples of these chains helps guide the model toward the desired method of reasoning.

concepts.name: Training distribution
concepts.definition: Training distribution is the underlying pattern of text co-occurrence found in the data, which models learn to represent in a finer-grained way as they become larger. This distribution dictates whether a model is likely to produce a truthful or a superstitious answer to a given query.

concepts.name: Instruction following
concepts.definition: Instruction following is the ability of a model to perform a specific task when given a detailed natural language instruction. This behavior requires focused fine-tuning and is not naturally achieved just by training on internet data.

concepts.name: In-context examples
concepts.definition: In-context examples are inputs included within a test query that the model uses to update its weights or train itself. These examples allow the model to perform supervised learning based on the provided context.

concepts.name: Next-word prediction objective
concepts.definition: Next-word prediction objective is the baseline training method where a model learns by predicting the next token in a sequence. This objective alone is insufficient to enable generic instruction-following.

concepts.name: Targeted supervision
concepts.definition: Targeted supervision is the process of providing models with specific, focused data on instruction-following tasks. This training method causes models to default to an instruction-following interpretation of inputs.

concepts.name: Chain-of-thought
concepts.definition: Chain-of-Thought is a reasoning or search process that an LLM performs itself, writing intermediate steps into its context and then continuing autoregressively. This process allows the language model to mimic a classical algorithm by generating the steps of a solution.

concepts.name: Context distillation
concepts.definition: Context distillation is a method of using synthetic data to transfer the behavior of a highly effective prompt into the model itself. This process allows the model to behave as if a good prompt were always present in the context without the user having to type it out.

concepts.name: Reinforcement learning from human feedback
concepts.definition: Reinforcement learning from human feedback is a third step in the language model training pipeline designed to control model output when the model's internal knowledge is unknown.

concepts.name: Reward model
concepts.definition: A reward model is a model trained using human annotations to reproduce judgments about which articles are good or bad. This model does not generate text, but instead scores the quality of generated content.

concepts.name: Policy
concepts.definition: Policy is a function that directly maps from a given state to the optimal action. This allows a neural network to predict the best action without needing to perform a search process.

concepts.name: Recognition problem
concepts.definition: Recognition problem generally refers to a task that is easier than a generation problem, both computationally and from a statistical efficiency standpoint. Recognition problems involve training models to score existing outputs, such as summaries, rather than generating new content.

concepts.name: Policy gradient
concepts.definition: Policy gradient is an algorithm used in reinforcement learning that transforms an objective function into a form resembling normal maximum likelihood estimation. This method weights each sample by the score assigned to it by a reward model, which is the core mechanism of reinforcement learning with human feedback.

concepts.name: Direct optimization
concepts.definition: Direct optimization is a learning method that avoids the need to train a separate reward model. Instead, it directly optimizes the language model to ensure that good outcomes have high probability and bad outcomes have low probability.

concepts.name: Series combination
concepts.definition: Series combination is a method of combining building blocks, which involves putting one component directly on top of another.

concepts.name: Parallel combination
concepts.definition: Parallel combination is a method of linking layers where the input is duplicated and sent to multiple pieces simultaneously, leading to a combined weight space and multiple outputs.

concepts.name: Sensitivity
concepts.definition: Sensitivity is a measure of how much the output of a layer changes when either the input is perturbed or the weights are perturbed.

concepts.name: Weight space
concepts.definition: Weight space is the specific set of parameters associated with an individual piece of the network. When multiple pieces are linked together, the weight spaces of those individual pieces are combined to form a combined weight space, with the nature of this combination depending on whether the pieces are arranged in series or parallel.

concepts.name: Loss function
concepts.definition: Loss function is a function (L symbol) that maps an n-dimensional parameter space to a real number. This function can be Taylor expanded, which includes first-order, Hessian, and higher-order terms.

concepts.name: Sharpness parameter lambda
concepts.definition: The sharpness parameter lambda is a parameter used alongside a norm to upper bound the second-order piece in the Taylor expansion.

concepts.name: Steepest descent optimization algorithm
concepts.definition: Steepest descent optimization algorithm is an optimization method that uses a specific norm to pick an update step, minimizing the linearization of the loss plus a penalty term involving the norm.

concepts.name: Composite loss function
concepts.definition: Composite loss function is a structure in deep learning where the total loss is formed by composing an error measure with the neural network. When both the error measure and the neural network are suitably differentiable, this structure allows for the Gauss-Newton decomposition of the second-order loss term.

concepts.name: Lipschitz smooth in its weights
concepts.definition: Lipschitz smooth in its weights is a condition requiring a norm on the weight space to upper bound a specific term in the Gauss-Newton decomposition. Although this property can be satisfied in any norm because all norms are equivalent, the choice of norm determines how tightly the guarantee holds.

concepts.name: Norm on the weight space
concepts.definition: Norm on the weight space is automatically constructed when composing individual layers and nonlinearities into a compound module. Using this norm enables normalization, which is claimed to improve training scaling without requiring learning rate adjustments.

concepts.name: Composition
concepts.definition: Composition is the process of combining modules, which automatically yields both the forward function and a norm on the weight space.

concepts.name: Concatenation
concepts.definition: Concatenation is a combination rule for modules that represents a parallel connection, allowing multiple modules to operate side-by-side.

concepts.name: Atoms
concepts.definition: Atoms are simple layers that are written manually by the developer, such as a linear layer, a convolution layer, or an embedding layer. Atoms represent the fundamental, basic building blocks of the system.

concepts.name: Compounds
concepts.definition: Compounds are structures that are created by combining other modules. Compounds represent complex systems built from the simpler components.

concepts.name: Sensitivity number
concepts.definition: Sensitivity number is a metric assigned to a module that measures the input-output sensitivity. Sensitivity number is defined as one of the Lipschitz constants.

concepts.name: Well-normed
concepts.definition: Well-normed refers to a module, such as a linear module, where the inputs and weights are bounded under specific norm choices. This boundedness is necessary to ensure Lipschitz guarantees and prevent the module from becoming arbitrarily sensitive.

concepts.name: Linear module
concepts.definition: A linear module is a classic component that performs a matrix vector multiplication. It is characterized by properties such as sensitivity and mass.

concepts.name: Embedding module
concepts.definition: An embedding module is a component that processes a one hot vector by selecting one of the columns of a matrix. This selection produces an embedding that corresponds to a specific token.

concepts.name: Well-normed module
concepts.definition: Well-normed module is a type of module that satisfies specific properties, ensuring that when modules are combined, the resulting module automatically maintains the well-normed property.

concepts.name: Tensor contraction
concepts.definition: Tensor contraction is a mathematical operation involving shared tensor indices, which serves as a shorthand for expressing various types of multiplication, such as a dot product or matrix multiplication.

concepts.name: Gradient
concepts.definition: Gradient is a dual vector that is primarily used for taking dot products with weights. It describes the linearization of the function.

concepts.name: Mass
concepts.definition: Mass is a degree of freedom that allows tuning how much one component, such as an embedding layer, is important relative to other components like residual blocks. Mass determines how much a block influences the features of any super module it contributes to during training.

concepts.name: Max norm
concepts.definition: Max norm is a specific norm chosen for the joint weight space when composing modules. This norm is used with special weighting coefficients to tune the importance of the two different modules in the composition.

concepts.name: Sharpness coefficient
concepts.definition: Sharpness coefficient is one of three coefficients used to characterize a module's sharpness, corresponding to varying just the weights, varying the weights and the input, or varying just the input. These coefficients can be thought of as a generalized notion of top eigenvalues.

concepts.name: Non-dimensional
concepts.definition: Non-dimensional describes a property where a constant, such as the Lipschitz constant, does not vary as the scale of the system changes. This fixed nature is required for successful scaling.

concepts.name: Weight updates
concepts.definition: Weight updates are the changes made to the network's parameters during training. Controlling the norm of these updates allows researchers to predict how much the outputs of the overall module will change.

concepts.name: Scaled spectral norm
concepts.definition: Scaled spectral norm is a specific type of norm that is effective for obtaining Lipschitz guarantees when applied to a linear layer.

concepts.name: Compound module
concepts.definition: Compound module is a structure, such as an MLP, that is built by combining individual layers and nonlinearities.

concepts.name: Duality map
concepts.definition: Duality map is the second component derived when decoupling the solutions of the optimization problem, specifically involving evaluation at argmax over a set of unit vectors.

concepts.name: Dual vector
concepts.definition: Dual vector is a linear map that takes a regular vector and returns a real number. Dual vectors are a concept in classical optimization theory that can be combined with regular vectors.

concepts.name: Linearization of the function
concepts.definition: Linearization of the function is the description of a function's local behavior, which the gradient provides by taking dot products with the weights. This is the only reliable information the gradient should be trusted to convey about the function.

concepts.name: Argmax
concepts.definition: Argmax is a procedure that seeks a step of unit norm which maximizes the linear improvement of the objective function. The solution to this procedure solves some kind of optimality criteria, which is determined by the norm chosen.

concepts.name: Inference
concepts.definition: Inference is the process of prediction, thinking, or reasoning when a user has a new query and seeks to understand the answer by thinking through things.

concepts.name: Training (a model)
concepts.definition: Training a model is the process of learning the properties of data by inferring the parameters that explain the data-generating process. This phase occurs before the model is used to address new problems in the wild.

concepts.name: Learning
concepts.definition: Learning is the process of coming up with a direct, feedforward heuristic mapping from data to answers, which is distinct from the extended-thinking process of inference.

concepts.name: Test-time training
concepts.definition: Test-time training is the process of updating a model's weights using data available during the testing phase. This allows the model to adapt its performance to a specific test scenario, even when only a single input is provided.

concepts.name: Train-time compute
concepts.definition: Train-time compute refers to the resources used during the training phase of a model. This includes increasing data volume, performing more iterations of gradient descent, or utilizing specific reinforcement learning training parts of the pipeline.

concepts.name: Test-time compute
concepts.definition: Test-time compute is the amount of computational power applied during inference or search through a model after it has been trained. This involves performing many passes through the model at test time.

concepts.name: Search
concepts.definition: Search is a method used in AI to look ahead through a chain of possibilities to determine the best possible action. Search involves exploring potential futures based on current game states.

concepts.name: Branching factor
concepts.definition: Branching factor is the number of possible moves that can be made at each position in a game. This factor determines the size of the search tree.

concepts.name: Trade-off curve
concepts.definition: Trade-off curve describes the relationship between search and learning capabilities. It shows that one can achieve a certain performance level by either increasing search or increasing training.

concepts.name: Autoregressive language model
concepts.definition: An autoregressive language model is a type of model that generates sequences one token at a time. The prediction for each subsequent token is conditioned on all the tokens that have already been sampled.

concepts.name: Autoregressive greedy sampling
concepts.definition: Autoregressive greedy sampling is a method where the model selects the most likely token at each step, given the tokens already chosen. This sequential selection process does not guarantee that the resulting sequence maximizes the joint probability of the entire sequence.

concepts.name: Joint probability
concepts.definition: Joint probability is the probability assigned by the model to an entire sequence of data. The goal of inference is to find the sequence that maximizes this joint probability.

concepts.name: Best-of-N approach
concepts.definition: Best-of-N approach is a method where one performs random sampling multiple times, and then evaluates the total likelihood of each generated sequence to select the highest probability result.

concepts.name: Temperature
concepts.definition: Temperature is a parameter that scales the categorical distribution, allowing the user to control whether the sampling is unbiased or if it is biased toward mode-seeking behavior.

concepts.name: Hill climbing
concepts.definition: Hill climbing is a method where you look for a local perturbation that improves the current solution. This approach differs from methods that attempt to improve the solution by modifying only one dimension of it at a time.

concepts.name: Best-of-N sampling
concepts.definition: Best-of-N sampling is a method where N independent samples are taken, and the single best result among them is selected, rejecting all others. This technique is noted as being about as effective as most advanced methods currently available.

concepts.name: Verification
concepts.definition: Verification is a popular scoring function where the output is checked for correctness using a formal process. This process might involve a compiler, a mathematical proof checker, or a dedicated verifier.

concepts.name: Verifier
concepts.definition: Verifier is a component that checks the output of a model, which can be an external system or another model. This allows the model to improve by learning from the verification process.

concepts.name: Best-of-N
concepts.definition: Best-of-N is a method used to select the optimal solution from multiple possibilities generated by a model. This selection is made by choosing the output that receives the highest score from the scoring function.

concepts.name: Supervised learning
concepts.definition: Supervised learning is the problem of taking a sequence of input-output (x, y) examples followed by a query and outputting the answer to the query.

concepts.name: Constrained optimization
concepts.definition: Constrained optimization is a process where the search is limited to specific variables, such as searching only over the latent variables rather than all possible pixels.

concepts.name: Multi-objective optimization
concepts.definition: Multi-objective optimization is the general field that studies how to manage a model when it has multiple competing goals, such as maximizing likelihood while also maximizing creativity.

concepts.name: Pareto frontier
concepts.definition: Pareto frontier is a set of optimal trade-off solutions in multi-objective optimization, representing the best possible balance between competing objectives without causing any other loss functions to decrease.

concepts.name: Loss function
concepts.definition: Loss function is a neural network trained to predict how likely a human is to remember an image, and it is fitted specifically to human data.

concepts.name: Manifold of high-probability images
concepts.definition: Manifold of high-probability images is the set of images that are highly probable according to the image generator, which is relevant when searching for images that match a specific text prompt.

concepts.name: Memorability
concepts.definition: Memorability is a subjective human perception that the research measures, often used in studies to determine how likely a person is to recall an image.

concepts.name: Individual differences
concepts.definition: Individual differences is a term in psychology referring to factors like culture, age, and individual characteristics that vary among people.

concepts.name: Chain-of-Thought paradigm
concepts.definition: Chain-of-Thought paradigm is a prompting paradigm where the model is instructed to perform symbolic search over reasoning that is written in natural language. This allows the model to execute sequential reasoning without requiring the reasoning process to be hard-coded.

concepts.name: Continuous reward optimization
concepts.definition: Continuous reward optimization is a method where the model is guided to produce outputs that match a desired reward function, such as an aesthetic level. The model learns a conditional distribution that dictates what the output should look like given the desired reward.

concepts.name: Prompting paradigm
concepts.definition: Prompting paradigm is a new method for optimizing and searching generative models by instructing the model rather than performing explicit search algorithms. This allows the user to ask the model to perform complex tasks, such as beam search, through language.

concepts.name: Emergent ability
concepts.definition: Emergent ability refers to learned capabilities of a model that are not guaranteed by well-understood search algorithms. These abilities depend entirely on how the model learned from the specific data distribution it was trained on.

concepts.name: Gradient descent over the context
concepts.definition: Gradient descent over the context is a proposed method involving gradient descent on queries without context, utilizing context examples solely to improve the mapping from the query directly to the answer.

concepts.name: Self-supervised test-time training
concepts.definition: Self-supervised test-time training is a method of test-time training that does not rely on supervised examples. Instead, the model learns by solving an unsupervised objective using the test input itself.

concepts.name: Masked autoencoder
concepts.definition: A Masked autoencoder is a self-supervised task where some patches of an input are removed. The model is then trained to predict the content of those missing patches.

concepts.name: Arc challenge
concepts.definition: Arc challenge is a difficult deep learning benchmark that presents a new query alongside a few in-context input-output examples. The challenge is designed to test a model's ability to find a pattern, often fooling older deep nets that relied only on general training rules.

concepts.name: Heuristic
concepts.definition: Heuristic is a learned prediction or rule that allows a system to estimate the quality of a state or move. This prediction is made without having to fully expand the search tree.
